questions.q: The time period $T$ of oscillation of a small liquid drop of radius $r$, density $\rho$, held together by surface tension $S$, is found using dimensional analysis to be proportional to
questions.explanation: Writing $T \propto \rho^a r^b S^c$ and matching $[M^0L^0T^1]$ with $[\rho]=[ML^{-3}]$, $[r]=[L]$, $[S]=[MT^{-2}]$ gives $a=\tfrac12$, $b=\tfrac32$, $c=-\tfrac12$, so $T \propto \sqrt{\rho r^3/S}$.
questions.trick: Set up $T\propto\rho^aS^br^c$, match $M^0L^0T^1$ to solve for exponents.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A screw gauge has pitch 0.5 mm and 50 divisions on its circular scale, with a positive zero error of 0.02 mm. While measuring a wire, the main scale reads 3 mm and the circular scale reads 20 divisions. The true diameter of the wire is
questions.explanation: L.C. $= 0.5/50 = 0.01$ mm. Observed reading $= 3 + 20\times0.01 = 3.20$ mm. True reading $=$ observed $-$ zero error $= 3.20 - 0.02 = 3.18$ mm.
questions.trick: True reading = observed $-$ zero error (positive error is always subtracted).
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Angular momentum has the same dimensional formula as
questions.explanation: Both angular momentum and Planck's constant have dimensions $[ML^2T^{-1}]$, while torque and work share $[ML^2T^{-2}]$ and power is $[ML^2T^{-3}]$.
questions.trick: Angular momentum = Planck's constant's dimensional twin, $[ML^2T^{-1}]$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Which of the following is an SI base unit, not a derived unit?
questions.explanation: Mole is one of the seven SI base units (amount of substance); newton, joule and watt are all derived from the base units.
questions.trick: Mole is one of the 7 SI base units; N, J, W are all derived.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The number of significant figures in $0.005080$ is
questions.explanation: Leading zeros are not significant. 5, 0, 8 and the trailing 0 after the decimal are significant → 4.
questions.trick: Leading zeros never count; count digits from first non-zero onward.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: If, with the jaws of a vernier caliper fully closed, the vernier zero lies to the right of the main scale zero, this is called a
questions.explanation: When the vernier zero is displaced to the right (positive side) of the main scale zero on closing the jaws, it is a positive zero error, and this reading must be subtracted from all measurements.
questions.trick: Vernier zero right of main-scale zero on closing = positive zero error (subtract it).
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A stone dropped from a tower reaches the ground in 4 s. The height of the tower is
questions.explanation: $h = \frac12gt^2 = \frac12\times10\times16 = 80$ m.
questions.trick: Free fall: $h=\frac12gt^2$, use $g=10$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A position–time (x–t) graph of a particle is a straight line inclined to the time axis. The particle is moving with
questions.explanation: A constant slope on an x–t graph means the velocity ($dx/dt$) does not change, i.e. uniform velocity.
questions.trick: Straight sloped line on x-t graph = constant slope = uniform velocity.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A car moving at 20 m s$^{-1}$ is brought to rest by brakes that produce a uniform deceleration of 5 m s$^{-2}$. The stopping distance is
questions.explanation: Using $v^2 = u^2 - 2as$ with $v=0$: $s = \dfrac{u^2}{2a} = \dfrac{400}{10} = 40$ m.
questions.trick: Stopping distance: $s=u^2/2a$ (set $v=0$ in $v^2=u^2-2as$).
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The slope of a velocity–time graph at any instant gives the instantaneous
questions.explanation: Slope of the v-t graph $= dv/dt$, which is the instantaneous acceleration.
questions.trick: Slope of v-t graph = acceleration.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The position of a particle is $x = 2t^2 + 3t + 1$ (in metres, $t$ in seconds). Its velocity at $t = 2$ s is
questions.trick: Differentiate $x(t)$ once for $v(t)$, then substitute $t$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A body starts from rest and moves with uniform acceleration 4 m s$^{-2}$. The distance covered by it in the 3rd second is
questions.trick: $n$th-second distance: $s_n=u+\frac{a}{2}(2n-1)$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Two vectors of magnitudes 2 units and 3 units are inclined at 30° to each other. The magnitude of their cross product is
questions.explanation: $|\vec A\times\vec B| = AB\sin\theta = 2\times3\times\sin30^\circ = 6\times0.5 = 3$.
questions.trick: $|\vec A\times\vec B|=AB\sin\theta$ — plug in directly.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: If $\vec A \cdot \vec B = 0$ and neither $\vec A$ nor $\vec B$ is a null vector, the angle between them is
questions.explanation: $\vec A\cdot\vec B = AB\cos\theta = 0$ with $A,B\neq0$ requires $\cos\theta = 0$, i.e. $\theta = 90^\circ$.
questions.trick: Zero dot product with nonzero vectors → they're perpendicular ($90^\circ$).
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A ball is projected with speed 20 m s$^{-1}$ at 60° to the horizontal. Its speed at the highest point of the trajectory is
questions.explanation: At the highest point only the horizontal component survives: $v = u\cos\theta = 20\times\cos60^\circ = 10$ m s$^{-1}$.
questions.trick: At the top, only horizontal component survives: $v=u\cos\theta$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A car of mass 1000 kg moves in a circular path of radius 50 m at a constant speed of 10 m s$^{-1}$. The centripetal force acting on it is
questions.trick: Centripetal force: $F=mv^2/r$ — direct plug-in.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A unit vector is a vector whose
options: magnitude equals that of a given vector
questions.explanation: A unit vector has magnitude exactly 1 and is used only to indicate direction; $\hat n = \vec A/|\vec A|$.
questions.trick: Unit vector: magnitude exactly 1, direction only.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A ball is thrown horizontally with a speed of 10 m s$^{-1}$ from the top of a 20 m high tower. The horizontal distance it covers before hitting the ground is
questions.explanation: Time to fall: $t=\sqrt{2h/g}=\sqrt{40/10}=2$ s. Horizontal range $= v_0t = 10\times2 = 20$ m.
questions.trick: Horizontal projectile: find fall time $t=\sqrt{2h/g}$, then range $=v_0t$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A man of mass 50 kg standing on a stationary 100 kg boat jumps off horizontally with a speed of 2 m s$^{-1}$ relative to the water. The recoil speed of the boat is
questions.explanation: Total momentum was zero: $M V = mv \Rightarrow V = \dfrac{50\times2}{100} = 1$ m s$^{-1}$, in the direction opposite to the man.
questions.trick: Zero initial momentum system: $MV=mv$ gives boat's recoil speed.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A cyclist goes round a circular track of radius 20 m at 10 m s$^{-1}$. The minimum coefficient of friction between tyres and road to avoid skidding is ($g = 10$ m s$^{-2}$)
questions.explanation: $\mu m g \ge \dfrac{mv^2}{r} \Rightarrow \mu \ge \dfrac{v^2}{rg} = \dfrac{100}{200} = 0.5$.
questions.trick: No-skid condition: $\mu\ge v^2/(rg)$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Two masses 5 kg and 3 kg are connected by a light string over a frictionless pulley. The acceleration of the system is ($g = 10$ m s$^{-2}$)
questions.trick: Atwood machine: $a=\dfrac{(m_1-m_2)g}{m_1+m_2}$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A horizontal force of 20 N is applied to a 3 kg block, which is in contact with and pushing a 2 kg block ahead of it along a frictionless floor. The contact force between the blocks is
questions.explanation: $a=F/(m_1+m_2)=20/5=4$ m s$^{-2}$. Contact force accelerates only the 2 kg block: $N=2\times4=8$ N.
questions.trick: Contact force = mass being pushed $\times$ common acceleration $a=F/(m_1+m_2)$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The inertia of a body is a measure of its
questions.explanation: Inertia (reluctance to change state of motion) increases with mass; a heavier body is harder to accelerate for a given force.
questions.trick: Inertia is measured by mass alone — not weight or volume.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A body of mass 2 kg has velocity $3\hat i$ m s$^{-1}$. After 2 s its velocity is $3\hat j$ m s$^{-1}$. The magnitude of the average force acting on it is
questions.explanation: $\Delta\vec v = 3\hat j - 3\hat i$, $|\Delta v| = 3\sqrt2$. $F = m|\Delta v|/t = 2\times3\sqrt2/2 = 3\sqrt2$ N.
questions.trick: Speed same, direction changed → find $|\Delta \vec v|$ via vector subtraction, not scalar difference.
questions.tip: Speed is unchanged but velocity (a vector) has changed — force is not zero.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A 2 kg block rests on top of a 3 kg block on a frictionless floor; the coefficient of friction between the two blocks is 0.4. A horizontal force F is applied to the lower (3 kg) block. The maximum value of F for which both blocks move together without slipping is ($g=10$ m s$^{-2}$)
questions.explanation: Friction must accelerate the top block: max $a = \mu g = 4$ m s$^{-2}$. Max $F = (m_1+m_2)a_{max} = 5\times4 = 20$ N.
questions.trick: Max common acceleration limited by friction on top block: $a_{max}=\mu g$, then $F_{max}=(m_1+m_2)a_{max}$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A lift accelerates downward at 2 m s$^{-2}$ carrying a 50 kg person standing on a weighing scale. The scale reading is ($g=10$ m s$^{-2}$)
questions.explanation: For downward acceleration, $N = m(g-a) = 50\times(10-2) = 400$ N.
questions.trick: Lift accelerating down: $N=m(g-a)$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A curved road of radius 100 m is banked at $45^\circ$. Ignoring friction, the safe speed for a vehicle is ($g = 10$ m s$^{-2}$)
questions.explanation: $v = \sqrt{rg\tan\theta} = \sqrt{100\times10\times1} = \sqrt{1000} = 10\sqrt{10}\approx31.6$ m s$^{-1}$.
questions.trick: Frictionless banking: $v=\sqrt{rg\tan\theta}$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A lift and everything inside it fall freely under gravity (cable snapped). The apparent weight of a person standing inside is
questions.explanation: In free fall, $a=g$, so $N=m(g-a)=0$: the person experiences weightlessness.
questions.trick: Free fall of lift ⇒ $a=g$ ⇒ apparent weight $N=0$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A bullet of mass 10 g is fired from a gun of mass 4 kg with a velocity of 400 m s$^{-1}$. The recoil velocity of the gun is
questions.explanation: Momentum conservation: $MV = mv \Rightarrow V = \dfrac{0.01\times400}{4} = 1$ m s$^{-1}$.
questions.trick: Recoil: $MV=mv$ — momentum conservation, opposite directions.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A body of mass 1 kg, initially at rest, has 50 J of net work done on it. Its final speed is
questions.explanation: By the work-energy theorem, $W = \frac12mv^2 \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{2W/m} = \sqrt{100} = 10$ m s$^{-1}$.
questions.trick: Work-energy theorem: $W=\frac12mv^2\Rightarrow v=\sqrt{2W/m}$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A particle moving along the x-axis is acted on by a force $F = 3x^2$ N (x in metres). The work done in moving it from $x=0$ to $x=2$ m is
questions.explanation: $W = \int_0^2 3x^2\,dx = \left[x^3\right]_0^2 = 8$ J.
questions.trick: Variable force work = $\int F\,dx$ over the given limits.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A stationary shell explodes into two fragments of masses 1 kg and 3 kg. The ratio of their kinetic energies (1 kg fragment : 3 kg fragment) is
questions.explanation: By momentum conservation the fragments have equal and opposite momenta ($p_1=p_2=p$). Since $KE=p^2/2m$, $KE_1:KE_2 = \dfrac{1}{m_1}:\dfrac{1}{m_2} = m_2:m_1 = 3:1$.
questions.trick: Explosion from rest: equal and opposite momenta → $KE\propto1/m$, so ratio is inverse of masses.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A spring of force constant 100 N m$^{-1}$ is stretched from 10 cm to 20 cm extension. The additional work done is
questions.trick: Spring work between two stretches: $W=\frac12k(x_2^2-x_1^2)$, not $\frac12k(x_2-x_1)^2$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The gravitational potential energy of a 3 kg mass held 4 m above the ground (taking the ground as reference) is
questions.explanation: $PE = mgh = 3\times10\times4 = 120$ J.
questions.trick: $PE=mgh$ — direct plug-in.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The work done by a conservative force on a particle that moves around any closed path and returns to its starting point is
questions.explanation: Zero net work over every closed path is the defining property of a conservative force.
questions.trick: Zero work over any closed loop is the hallmark of a conservative force.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A rotating disc of moment of inertia 6 kg m$^2$ spinning at 2 rad s$^{-1}$ deforms (with no external torque) so that its moment of inertia becomes 3 kg m$^2$. Its new angular velocity is
questions.explanation: Angular momentum is conserved: $I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2 \Rightarrow 6\times2 = 3\times\omega_2 \Rightarrow \omega_2 = 4$ rad s$^{-1}$.
questions.trick: Angular momentum conserved: $I_1\omega_1=I_2\omega_2$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A solid sphere rolls without slipping down a rough incline of angle 30°. Its linear acceleration is ($g=10$ m s$^{-2}$)
questions.explanation: $a = \dfrac{g\sin\theta}{1+k^2/R^2} = \dfrac{10\times0.5}{1+2/5} = \dfrac{5}{1.4} \approx 3.57$ m s$^{-2}$.
questions.trick: Rolling acceleration down incline: $a=\dfrac{g\sin\theta}{1+k^2/R^2}$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The total kinetic energy of a solid sphere of mass $m$ rolling without slipping with centre-of-mass speed $v$ is
questions.explanation: $KE = \frac12mv^2 + \frac12I\omega^2 = \frac12mv^2\left(1+\dfrac{k^2}{R^2}\right)$; for a solid sphere $k^2/R^2 = 2/5$, giving $KE = \frac{7}{10}mv^2$.
questions.trick: Solid sphere rolling KE $=\frac{7}{10}mv^2$ — memorise the rolling-KE table.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The moment of inertia of a rigid body about a given axis depends on
options: only the total mass of the body
only the shape of the body
only the axis chosen, regardless of the mass
the mass and how it is distributed relative to the axis of rotation
questions.explanation: $I=\sum m_ir_i^2$ depends on both how much mass there is and how far each part lies from the chosen axis.
questions.trick: Moment of inertia depends on both mass AND its distribution about the axis.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The torque $\vec\tau = \vec r\times\vec F$ acting on a particle is directed
options: along the resultant of $\vec r$ and $\vec F$
perpendicular to the plane containing $\vec r$ and $\vec F$
questions.explanation: The cross product of two vectors is always perpendicular to the plane containing them, direction given by the right-hand rule.
questions.trick: Cross product $\vec r\times\vec F$ is always perpendicular to both vectors' plane.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A couple is best described as
options: a pair of equal, opposite, parallel, non-collinear forces producing pure rotation without translation
a single force that produces rotation
any two forces acting on a rigid body
two equal and opposite forces acting along the same line
questions.explanation: A couple consists of two equal and opposite forces whose lines of action do not coincide; it produces a net torque but zero net force, so it rotates the body without translating it.
questions.trick: A couple = equal, opposite, non-collinear forces → pure rotation, zero net force.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A torque of 5 N m acts on a body, rotating it through one complete revolution ($2\pi$ rad). The work done by the torque is
questions.explanation: $W = \tau\theta = 5\times2\pi \approx 31.4$ J.
questions.trick: Rotational work: $W=\tau\theta$ (analogous to $W=Fd$).
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A wheel of moment of inertia 4 kg m$^2$ rotates with angular velocity 3 rad s$^{-1}$. Its rotational kinetic energy is
questions.explanation: $KE_{rot} = \frac12I\omega^2 = \frac12\times4\times9 = 18$ J.
questions.trick: Rotational KE: $\frac12I\omega^2$ — direct plug-in.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A uniform disc of mass 4 kg and radius 0.5 m has moment of inertia 0.5 kg m² about the central axis perpendicular to its plane. Using the perpendicular axis theorem, its moment of inertia about a diameter is
questions.explanation: By symmetry $I_x=I_y$ for the two perpendicular diameters, and $I_x+I_y=I_z \Rightarrow I_x = I_z/2 = 0.5/2 = 0.25$ kg m².
questions.trick: Perpendicular axis theorem: by symmetry $I_x=I_y=I_z/2$ for a disc's diameter.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The moment of inertia of a uniform thin rod of mass $M$ and length $L$ about an axis through its centre, perpendicular to its length, is
questions.explanation: Standard result for a thin rod about its centre: $I = \dfrac{ML^2}{12}$.
questions.trick: Thin rod about centre: $I=\dfrac{ML^2}{12}$ — memorise.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The moment of inertia of a thin spherical shell (hollow sphere) of mass M and radius R about a diameter is
questions.explanation: For a thin hollow spherical shell about a diameter, $I = \frac23MR^2$ (larger than a solid sphere's $\frac25MR^2$ since the mass lies farther from the axis).
questions.trick: Hollow sphere about diameter: $I=\frac23MR^2$ (bigger than solid sphere's $\frac25$).
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The Moon has about 1/4 the Earth's radius and about 1/6 its surface gravity. If Earth's escape velocity is 11.2 km/s, the Moon's escape velocity is closest to
questions.explanation: $v_e=\sqrt{2gR}$, so $v_{e,\text{moon}}/v_{e,\text{earth}} = \sqrt{(1/6)(1/4)} = \sqrt{1/24}\approx0.204$; $0.204\times11.2\approx2.3$ km/s.
questions.trick: $v_e=\sqrt{2gR}$: combine the given ratios of $g$ and $R$ under one square root.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Two point masses of 2 kg and 3 kg are placed 1 m apart. The gravitational force of attraction between them ($G = 6.67\times10^{-11}$ N m$^2$ kg$^{-2}$) is approximately
questions.explanation: $F = \dfrac{Gm_1m_2}{r^2} = \dfrac{6.67\times10^{-11}\times2\times3}{1^2} \approx 4\times10^{-10}$ N.
questions.trick: $F=Gm_1m_2/r^2$ — direct plug-in.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Two planets orbit the Sun with orbital radii in the ratio 4 : 1. The ratio of their time periods is
questions.explanation: By Kepler's third law $T \propto r^{3/2}$, so $T_1/T_2 = (r_1/r_2)^{3/2} = 4^{3/2} = 8$.
questions.trick: Kepler's third law: $T\propto r^{3/2}$, so ratio 4:1 in $r$ gives $4^{1.5}=8$ in $T$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The acceleration due to gravity on the Earth's surface is slightly less at the equator than at the poles. This is mainly due to
options: Earth's rotation and its equatorial bulge, both of which reduce effective g at the equator
the Moon being closer to the equator
atmospheric pressure being higher at the equator
the Sun's gravitational pull being stronger at the equator
questions.explanation: Earth's rotation produces an outward effect greatest at the equator, and the equatorial radius is also larger due to the bulge (g \propto 1/R^2); both effects lower g there compared to the poles.
questions.trick: Equator vs pole $g$ difference: rotation's outward effect + equatorial bulge, both reduce $g$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: For an artificial satellite moving in a stable circular orbit, its kinetic energy $K$ and potential energy $U$ are related by
questions.explanation: $K=\dfrac{GMm}{2r}$ and $U=-\dfrac{GMm}{r}=-2K$.
questions.trick: Orbiting satellite always has $U=-2K$ — a fixed relation worth memorising.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Treating the Earth as a uniform solid sphere, the acceleration due to gravity at its centre is
options: equal to the surface value g
questions.explanation: $g' = g(1-d/R)$; at the centre $d=R$, so $g'=0$. Only the mass enclosed within radius $r$ contributes, and none is enclosed at $r=0$.
questions.trick: At Earth's centre, enclosed mass is zero → $g=0$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Using $Y=3K(1-2\sigma)$, if a material has bulk modulus $K=1.6\times10^{11}$ Pa and Poisson's ratio $\sigma=0.25$, its Young's modulus is
questions.trick: Recall $Y=3K(1-2\sigma)$ — a direct plug-in relation between moduli.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A wire of length 2 m, cross-sectional area $1\times10^{-6}$ m$^2$ and Young's modulus $2\times10^{11}$ Pa is stretched by a force of 100 N. Its elongation is
questions.explanation: $\Delta L = \dfrac{FL}{AY} = \dfrac{100\times2}{(1\times10^{-6})(2\times10^{11})} = \dfrac{200}{2\times10^{5}} = 1\times10^{-3}$ m = 1 mm.
questions.trick: $\Delta L=FL/(AY)$ — direct substitution, no need to find $Y$ separately.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A wire of length 1 m and cross-sectional area 1 mm$^2$ stretches by 0.5 mm under a load of 100 N. Its Young's modulus is
questions.explanation: $Y = \dfrac{FL}{A\Delta L} = \dfrac{100\times1}{(1\times10^{-6})(5\times10^{-4})} = \dfrac{100}{5\times10^{-10}} = 2\times10^{11}$ Pa.
questions.trick: $Y=FL/(A\Delta L)$: plug values, watch mm$^2\to$m$^2$ and mm$\to$m conversions.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: On the stress-strain graph of a ductile metal, the region just after the yield point, where the material continues to elongate substantially even though the stress increases only slightly, is called
questions.explanation: Beyond the yield point, the material deforms plastically with large increases in strain for only small increases in stress, until it reaches the ultimate tensile strength and eventually fractures.
questions.trick: Big strain jump for tiny stress rise right after yield = plastic region.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Two wires of the same material and cross-sectional area, but of lengths $L$ and $2L$, are stretched by the same load. The ratio of their elongations (shorter : longer) is
questions.explanation: $\Delta L = FL/(AY) \propto L$ for fixed $F, A, Y$, so the elongations are in the ratio $L:2L = 1:2$.
questions.trick: $\Delta L\propto L$ for same $F,A,Y$ — ratio equals length ratio.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Young's modulus of most metals
options: becomes infinite at very high temperature
questions.explanation: Increasing temperature generally weakens interatomic bonding forces, reducing the material's stiffness, so Young's modulus decreases with rising temperature for most metals.
questions.trick: Heat weakens interatomic bonds $\Rightarrow$ $Y$ falls as temperature rises.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Water rises to a height of 3 cm in a capillary tube of radius 0.5 mm ($\rho=1000$ kg m$^{-3}$, $g=10$ m s$^{-2}$, angle of contact $\approx0°$). The surface tension of water is approximately
questions.explanation: $T=\dfrac{h\rho g r}{2\cos\theta}=\dfrac{0.03\times1000\times10\times0.0005}{2}=0.075$ N/m.
questions.trick: $T=h\rho gr/(2\cos\theta)$ — rearranged capillary-rise formula, plug and simplify.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Two soap bubbles of different radii, formed at the two ends of a tube with a stopcock, are connected by opening the stopcock. Air flows from the smaller bubble into the larger one until the smaller one collapses. This happens because
options: the smaller bubble has a higher excess internal pressure ($\Delta P = 4T/r$, inversely proportional to $r$), so air flows from it to the lower-pressure larger bubble
surface tension always favours the larger bubble growing at the expense of any smaller one, regardless of pressure
the larger bubble has a lower surface tension
the smaller bubble has a lower internal pressure and forces air out
questions.explanation: Since $\Delta P=4T/r$, a smaller radius gives a larger excess pressure; air therefore flows from the high-pressure smaller bubble into the larger, lower-pressure one until the smaller bubble empties and collapses.
questions.trick: Smaller bubble has higher $\Delta P=4T/r$ $\Rightarrow$ air flows small $\to$ large.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: For flow to remain laminar (streamlined) in a pipe, the Reynolds number should be
questions.explanation: $R_e = \rho vd/\eta$; flow is laminar for $R_e$ below roughly 1000 and turbulent above about 2000, with an unstable region in between.
questions.trick: Recall cutoffs: $R_e<1000$ laminar, $R_e>2000$ turbulent, in between unstable.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Adding detergent to water lowers its surface tension. As a result, the height to which the soapy water rises in a fine capillary tube, compared to pure water, is
options: infinite, since soap solutions do not obey the capillary rise formula
questions.explanation: $h=\dfrac{2T\cos\theta}{\rho g r}$; a lower surface tension $T$ directly gives a smaller rise $h$.
questions.trick: $h\propto T$ directly (capillary rise) — lower $T$ from detergent means smaller $h$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: An aircraft wing is shaped (cambered) so that air moves faster over its curved upper surface than beneath it. By Bernoulli's principle, this produces
options: increased drag but no vertical force
a net upward force (lift), because the faster-moving air above the wing is at lower pressure than the slower air below
a downward force pulling the aircraft toward the ground
no net force, since both surfaces experience identical pressure
questions.explanation: Faster flow over the top means lower pressure there (Bernoulli's theorem); the resulting pressure difference produces the net upward lift force.
questions.trick: Faster air on top (Bernoulli) $\Rightarrow$ lower pressure there $\Rightarrow$ net lift up.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The excess pressure inside a soap bubble of radius $r$ and surface tension $T$ is
questions.explanation: A soap bubble has two free surfaces (inner and outer film surfaces), so $\Delta P = 4T/r$, unlike a liquid drop which has only one surface ($2T/r$).
questions.trick: Soap bubble has two surfaces $\Rightarrow\Delta P=4T/r$ (drop: $2T/r$).
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The heat required to convert 10 g of ice at 0°C completely into water at 0°C (latent heat of fusion of ice $=3.34\times10^5$ J kg$^{-1}$) is
questions.explanation: $Q = mL = 0.01\times3.34\times10^5 = 3340$ J. No temperature change occurs during melting.
questions.trick: $Q=mL$ for phase change — no $\Delta T$ term, temperature stays fixed.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A pressure cooker cooks food faster than an open pan mainly because
options: the cooker material has unusually high thermal conductivity
increasing pressure inside lowers the boiling point of water, so it boils at a lower temperature and cooks faster
the sealed lid increases the specific heat of water
increasing pressure inside raises the boiling point of water, so cooking occurs at a higher temperature
questions.explanation: Boiling point rises with increasing pressure; the sealed cooker traps steam, raising the internal pressure and hence the temperature at which water boils, cooking food faster.
questions.trick: Pressure cooker: higher internal pressure raises boiling point, cooks faster at higher $T$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Two rods of the same material, length and temperature difference across their ends, but cross-sectional areas $A$ and $2A$, conduct heat independently in parallel between the same hot and cold reservoirs. The ratio of the heat currents through them (thinner : thicker) is
questions.explanation: Heat current $=KA\Delta T/L \propto A$ for fixed $K,L,\Delta T$, so the ratio of currents equals the ratio of areas, $A:2A=1:2$.
questions.trick: Parallel rods: heat current $\propto A$ (same $K,L,\Delta T$) — ratio equals area ratio.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A bimetallic strip made of brass and iron (brass having a higher coefficient of linear expansion) bends towards the iron side on heating because
options: brass expands more than iron, so the strip curves with brass on the outside
questions.explanation: On heating, brass (higher $\alpha$) elongates more than iron, forcing the strip to curve with brass forming the outer (longer) arc, i.e. the strip bends towards the iron side.
questions.trick: Higher-$\alpha$ metal (brass) elongates more, forming the outer arc of the curve.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A body cools from 60°C to 50°C in 10 minutes when the surrounding temperature is 30°C. By Newton's law of cooling, the average rate of fall of temperature depends on
options: the absolute temperature of the body only
the excess of average body temperature over surrounding temperature
the specific heat of the surroundings
the mass of the body only
questions.explanation: Newton's law of cooling states the rate of cooling is proportional to the difference between the (average) body temperature and the surrounding temperature.
questions.trick: Rate of cooling $\propto$ (average body temp $-$ surrounding temp), per Newton's law.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The energy radiated per second per unit area by a black body is proportional to
questions.explanation: Stefan-Boltzmann law: $E = \sigma T^4$.
questions.trick: Stefan-Boltzmann: $E=\sigma T^4$ — fourth power, not squared or cubed.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A refrigerator works between 260 K (freezer) and 300 K (room). Its coefficient of performance is
questions.trick: $\text{COP}=T_2/(T_1-T_2)$ — plug the cold and hot reservoir temperatures.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A gas expands from the same initial state to the same final volume, once isothermally and once adiabatically. Compared to the isothermal case, the final pressure reached after the adiabatic expansion is
questions.explanation: Since the adiabatic curve is steeper than the isothermal curve through the same initial point ($PV^\gamma$ falls off faster than $PV=$ const), for the same volume increase the adiabatic final pressure is lower.
questions.trick: Same starting point, same $V$: adiabatic curve falls steeper $\Rightarrow$ lower final $P$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A reversible thermodynamic process is one that
options: can only occur in a vacuum
always releases heat to the surroundings
can be exactly retraced in the reverse direction, restoring both the system and surroundings to their original states, and consists of a succession of equilibrium states
questions.explanation: A reversible process proceeds through a continuous series of equilibrium states with no dissipative effects (friction, unrestrained expansion), so reversing it restores the initial state of both system and surroundings exactly.
questions.trick: Reversible = retraceable exactly, passing only through equilibrium states throughout.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: For a diatomic ideal gas with $\gamma=1.4$ and $R=8.3$ J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$, using $C_V=\dfrac{R}{\gamma-1}$, the molar specific heat at constant volume is
questions.trick: $C_V=R/(\gamma-1)$ — direct formula linking $\gamma$ and $C_V$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Two moles of a diatomic ideal gas ($\gamma=7/5$, $R=8.3$ J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$) expand adiabatically, and its temperature falls from 400 K to 300 K. The work done by the gas is
questions.explanation: $W=\dfrac{nR(T_1-T_2)}{\gamma-1}=\dfrac{2\times8.3\times100}{0.4}=4150$ J.
questions.trick: Adiabatic work $W=nR(T_1-T_2)/(\gamma-1)$ — direct formula, plug and go.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Unlike solids and liquids, an ideal gas does not have a single fixed specific heat capacity because
options: the specific heat of a gas depends on the process (e.g. constant volume vs constant pressure) it undergoes, since the work done varies with the path taken
questions.explanation: Because $Q=\Delta U+W$ and $W$ depends on the process followed, the heat needed to raise a gas's temperature by a given amount (and hence its specific heat) differs for, say, constant-volume and constant-pressure heating.
questions.trick: Gas specific heat isn't fixed because $W$ (hence $Q$) depends on the process.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The ratio of the average speed to the rms speed of gas molecules, $v_{avg}/v_{rms}$, using $v_{avg}=\sqrt{8RT/\pi M}$ and $v_{rms}=\sqrt{3RT/M}$, is
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{v_{avg}}{v_{rms}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{8/\pi}{3}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{8}{3\pi}}\approx\sqrt{0.849}\approx0.92$.
questions.trick: $v_{avg}/v_{rms}=\sqrt{8/(3\pi)}\approx0.92$ — a fixed numeric ratio, memorise.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: At the same temperature, the ratio of rms speeds of hydrogen (M = 2 g/mol) and oxygen (M = 32 g/mol) molecules is
questions.explanation: $v_{rms}\propto1/\sqrt M$; ratio $=\sqrt{32/2}=\sqrt{16}=4$, so hydrogen:oxygen $=4:1$.
questions.trick: $v_{rms}\propto1/\sqrt M$ — ratio $=\sqrt{M_2/M_1}$, lighter gas is faster.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: At very high temperatures, a diatomic gas molecule can also vibrate along the bond, adding 2 more degrees of freedom (kinetic + potential) to the usual 5 (translational + rotational). The total number of degrees of freedom then becomes
questions.explanation: 3 translational + 2 rotational + 2 vibrational $=7$ degrees of freedom at sufficiently high temperature.
questions.trick: Add 2 vibrational DOF to rigid diatomic's 5 $\Rightarrow$ 7 DOF at high $T$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: At constant volume, when the temperature of a gas is increased, its pressure increases mainly because the gas molecules
options: start attracting the walls of the container more strongly
move faster on average and collide with the container walls more frequently and with a greater change in momentum per collision
questions.explanation: Higher temperature means higher average molecular speed; both the collision frequency with the walls and the momentum transferred per collision increase, raising the pressure, consistent with $P\propto T$ at constant volume.
questions.trick: Higher $T\Rightarrow$ faster molecules $\Rightarrow$ more frequent, harder wall collisions $\Rightarrow P$ up.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The mean free path of gas molecules $\lambda = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt2\,n\pi d^2}$. If the number density $n$ of the gas is doubled (temperature constant), the mean free path becomes
questions.explanation: $\lambda \propto 1/n$, so doubling the number density halves the mean free path.
questions.trick: $\lambda\propto1/n$ — double the number density, halve the mean free path.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Two gases at the same temperature have densities $\rho_1$ and $\rho_2$ and pressures $P_1$ and $P_2$ respectively. If $P_1=P_2$, then according to $P=\tfrac13\rho\overline{v^2}$, the mean square speeds are related as $\rho_1\overline{v_1^2}=\rho_2\overline{v_2^2}$. This is consistent with rms speed being
options: inversely proportional to $\sqrt{\text{density}}$ at fixed pressure
questions.explanation: From $P=\tfrac13\rho v_{rms}^2$, at fixed $P$, $v_{rms}=\sqrt{3P/\rho}\propto1/\sqrt\rho$.
questions.trick: From $P=\frac13\rho v_{rms}^2$ at fixed $P$: $v_{rms}\propto1/\sqrt\rho$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A simple pendulum is taken to the surface of the Moon, where $g$ is about $1/6$ of that on Earth. Its time period on the Moon compared to Earth becomes approximately
questions.explanation: $T\propto1/\sqrt g$; with $g$ reduced to $1/6$, $T$ increases by a factor of $\sqrt6$.
questions.trick: $T\propto1/\sqrt g$ — smaller $g$ (Moon) means $T$ grows by $\sqrt6$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: In damped oscillations, the amplitude of oscillation
questions.explanation: A resistive (damping) force dissipates energy continuously, causing the amplitude to decrease exponentially with time.
questions.trick: Damping $\Rightarrow$ amplitude decays exponentially, $A(t)=A_0e^{-bt/2m}$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Two simple pendulums of lengths $l$ and $4l$ are set up at the same location. The ratio of their time periods $T_1:T_2$ is
questions.explanation: $T\propto\sqrt l$, so $T_1:T_2=\sqrt l:\sqrt{4l}=1:2$.
questions.trick: $T\propto\sqrt l$ — ratio of periods is square root of the length ratio.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A particle executes SHM as $x=A\sin(\omega t+\phi)$. At $t=0$, it is at $x=A/2$ and moving in the positive direction. The initial phase $\phi$ is
questions.explanation: At $t=0$: $\sin\phi=1/2$, giving $\phi=\pi/6$ or $5\pi/6$. Since velocity $v=A\omega\cos\phi$ is positive, $\cos\phi>0$, which selects $\phi=\pi/6$.
questions.trick: $\sin\phi=1/2$ and $\cos\phi>0$ (moving positive) together pick $\phi=\pi/6$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A mass hung from a vertical spring produces a static extension $e$. The angular frequency of its vertical oscillations is
questions.explanation: At equilibrium $ke=mg \Rightarrow k/m=g/e$; since $\omega=\sqrt{k/m}$, $\omega=\sqrt{g/e}$.
questions.trick: Static extension trick: $\omega=\sqrt{g/e}$ since $k/m=g/e$ at equilibrium.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A block of mass 0.1 kg is attached to a spring of force constant 10 N/m and set into oscillation. Its time period is approximately
questions.explanation: $T=2\pi\sqrt{m/k}=2\pi\sqrt{0.1/10}=2\pi\times0.1\approx0.628$ s.
questions.trick: $T=2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$ — plug values directly, $\sqrt{0.1/10}=0.1$ gives clean answer.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: In a stationary wave pattern, the points of zero displacement at all times are called
questions.explanation: Nodes are points of permanent zero displacement in a stationary wave; antinodes are points of maximum amplitude of vibration.
questions.trick: Nodes = permanent zero displacement; antinodes = maximum displacement points.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in its third harmonic. The total number of nodes (including the two fixed ends) is
questions.explanation: The $n$th harmonic of a string fixed at both ends has $(n+1)$ nodes and $n$ antinodes; for $n=3$, nodes $=4$.
questions.trick: $n$th harmonic of fixed-fixed string has $(n+1)$ nodes — third harmonic gives 4.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Two points on a wave have a path difference of $\lambda/4$. The corresponding phase difference between them is
questions.explanation: Phase difference $\Delta\phi = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\times\dfrac{\lambda}{4}=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
questions.trick: Phase diff $=(2\pi/\lambda)\times$path diff — plug $\lambda/4$ directly for $\pi/2$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The SI unit of frequency of a wave is
questions.explanation: Frequency, the number of oscillations per second, is measured in hertz (Hz).
questions.trick: Frequency's SI unit is always hertz (Hz), oscillations per second.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: An observer moves towards a stationary source of sound with speed $v_o$. The apparent frequency heard is
questions.explanation: When the observer approaches a stationary source, apparent frequency $f'=f\dfrac{v+v_o}{v}$, which is greater than $f$.
questions.trick: Observer approaching stationary source: $f'=f(v+v_o)/v$ — numerator grows.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A tuning fork of unknown frequency produces 4 beats per second with a standard fork of frequency 256 Hz. When the unknown fork is loaded with wax, the beat frequency decreases. The frequency of the unknown fork is
questions.explanation: Loading with wax decreases the unknown fork's frequency. Since the beat frequency decreased, the unknown frequency must have been above 256 Hz, moving closer to it: $f=256+4=260$ Hz.
questions.trick: Wax lowers frequency; beats decreasing means unknown was above standard: add 4.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Inside a uniformly charged hollow conducting sphere, the electric field is
options: equal to the field at the surface
inversely proportional to distance from centre
questions.explanation: All charge resides on the outer surface; a Gaussian surface inside encloses zero charge, so $E=0$ inside.
questions.trick: Hollow conductor: charge only on outer surface → inside field is always zero.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The SI unit of electric dipole moment is
questions.explanation: $p = q\times(2a)$, product of charge (C) and separation (m), so unit is C m.
questions.trick: Dipole moment unit: charge $\times$ distance = C m, remember it's not C m$^2$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Electric field lines around an isolated positive point charge are
questions.explanation: Field lines originate on positive charge and point radially outward in all directions.
questions.trick: Positive point charge: field lines are straight and radially outward, always.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Two point charges 2 $\mu$C and 8 $\mu$C are separated by 30 cm in air. The electrostatic force between them is nearly
questions.explanation: $F = k\dfrac{q_1q_2}{r^2} = \dfrac{9\times10^9\times2\times10^{-6}\times8\times10^{-6}}{0.09} = \dfrac{0.144}{0.09} = 1.6\,\text{N}$.
questions.trick: Plug into $F=kq_1q_2/r^2$ directly; convert cm to m first, don't forget.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A solid sphere of radius $R$ carries a total charge $Q$ uniformly distributed through its volume. The electric field at a distance $r = R/2$ from the centre is
questions.explanation: Inside a uniformly charged solid sphere, $E = kQr/R^3$. At $r=R/2$: $E = kQ(R/2)/R^3 = kQ/(2R^2)$.
questions.trick: Inside solid sphere $E\propto r$: use $E=kQr/R^3$, not $kQ/r^2$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Two small identical conducting spheres carry charges $6\,\mu$C and $-2\,\mu$C. They are brought into contact and then separated. The charge on each sphere now is
questions.explanation: On contact, identical conductors share total charge equally: $(6+(-2))/2 = 2\,\mu$C each.
questions.trick: Identical conductors touching: charge splits equally, total$/2$ each.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The electric field just outside the surface of a charged conductor with surface charge density $\sigma$ is
questions.explanation: For a conductor surface, $E = \sigma/\varepsilon_0$ (twice the field of an isolated infinite sheet of the same $\sigma$).
questions.trick: Conductor surface field is $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$ — double the isolated-sheet value.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: According to Gauss's law, the electric flux through a closed surface depends on
options: charges both inside and outside the surface
questions.explanation: Gauss's law states $\phi = q_{enc}/\varepsilon_0$, independent of the surface's shape or size and unaffected by charges outside it.
questions.trick: Gauss's law: flux depends ONLY on enclosed charge — ignore shape/size/outside charges.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: An electric dipole placed in a uniform electric field is in stable equilibrium when the angle between $\vec p$ and $\vec E$ is
questions.explanation: $U=-pE\cos\theta$ is minimum (most stable) at $\theta=0^\circ$, when $\vec p$ is aligned with $\vec E$.
questions.trick: Stable equilibrium: $\vec p\parallel\vec E$, i.e. $\theta=0^\circ$, minimum $U=-pE$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Two equal point charges placed at two corners of a right angle exert forces $F$ each, mutually perpendicular, on a third charge kept at the right-angle vertex. The net force on the third charge is
questions.explanation: The resultant of two equal, mutually perpendicular vectors of magnitude $F$ is $\sqrt{F^2+F^2}=F\sqrt2$.
questions.trick: Perpendicular equal forces combine as $F\sqrt2$ (Pythagoras), not $2F$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A rod of length 20 cm carries a uniformly distributed charge of 4 $\mu$C. Its linear charge density is
questions.trick: $\lambda=q/l$ — straightforward division, watch cm-to-m conversion.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The net electric field at a point due to a group of point charges is obtained by
options: scalar addition of the magnitudes of individual fields
vector addition of the fields due to each charge, treating others as absent
questions.explanation: By the superposition principle, the resultant field is the vector sum of the fields each charge would independently produce at that point.
questions.trick: Superposition = vector sum of individual fields, each as if others didn't exist.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A point charge $+q$ is kept 10 cm from another point charge $-q$. The electric field at the midpoint of the line joining them is directed
options: perpendicular to the line joining charges
zero, since charges are equal and opposite
from $+q$ to $-q$, magnitude $8kq/r_0^2$ where $r_0$ is total separation
questions.explanation: At the midpoint, fields due to $+q$ (pointing away, toward $-q$) and $-q$ (pointing toward it, same direction) add up: each contributes $kq/(r_0/2)^2 = 4kq/r_0^2$, total $8kq/r_0^2$, directed from $+q$ towards $-q$.
questions.trick: Midpoint of $+q,-q$: both fields point the same way (+ to −), so they ADD, not cancel.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: An electric dipole is placed in a non-uniform electric field. It experiences
options: neither a net force nor a torque
only a net force, never a torque
both a net force and (in general) a torque
only a torque, never a net force
questions.explanation: In a non-uniform field the forces on the two ends of the dipole are unequal, producing a net force, and in general also a net torque (in a uniform field only a torque acts, with zero net force).
questions.trick: Non-uniform field on a dipole: net force AND torque both act (uniform field: only torque).
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Three point charges $+q$, $+q$ and $-2q$ are placed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle. The net charge enclosed relevant to Gauss's law for a sphere surrounding all three is
questions.explanation: Net enclosed charge $= q+q-2q = 0$, so total outward flux through the enclosing surface is zero (field need not be zero everywhere on it).
questions.trick: Just algebraically sum the charges for enclosed-charge questions: $q+q-2q=0$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A body acquires a charge of $3.2\times10^{-18}$ C. The number of electrons it must have gained is
questions.trick: $n=q/e$ — divide charge by $1.6\times10^{-19}$ C.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The direction of the electric dipole moment vector $\vec p$ of a dipole is
options: from the negative charge to the positive charge
perpendicular to the line joining the charges
along the external electric field always
from the positive charge to the negative charge
questions.explanation: By convention, $\vec p$ points from the negative charge towards the positive charge, along the dipole axis.
questions.trick: $\vec p$ points negative → positive, by definition — opposite to conventional current-in-a-wire intuition.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A dipole of moment $2\times10^{-8}$ C m is placed in a uniform field of $5\times10^4$ N/C, initially aligned along the field. The work done to rotate it through $180^\circ$ is
questions.explanation: $W = U(180^\circ)-U(0^\circ) = pE - (-pE) = 2pE = 2\times2\times10^{-8}\times5\times10^4 = 2\times10^{-3}$ J.
questions.trick: $180^\circ$ flip work is always $2pE$ — a shortcut worth memorising.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: An electric dipole of dipole moment $p$ is placed in a uniform electric field $E$ with its axis making $60^\circ$ with the field. The torque on it is
questions.explanation: $\tau = pE\sin\theta = pE\sin60^\circ = pE\sqrt3/2$.
questions.trick: $\tau=pE\sin\theta$; $\sin60^\circ=\sqrt3/2$, memorise the standard angles.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A charge $q$ is placed at the centre of a cube. If the charge is now moved to one corner of the cube (still inside), the total electric flux through the whole cube surface
questions.explanation: Total flux through a closed surface depends only on enclosed charge ($q/\varepsilon_0$), regardless of the charge's position inside.
questions.trick: Total flux depends only on enclosed charge, not its position inside — unchanged.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Which of the following is a correct property of electric charge?
options: charge can take any arbitrary (non-quantised) value
total charge of an isolated system remains conserved
charge is not conserved in an isolated system
questions.explanation: Charge is a conserved, quantised, additive scalar quantity; like charges repel, they do not attract.
questions.trick: Charge properties: quantised, additive, conserved; like charges REPEL not attract.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A parallel plate capacitor has plate area 0.02 m$^2$ and separation 2 mm. Its capacitance in air is (take $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}$ F/m)
questions.trick: $C=\varepsilon_0A/d$ — plug straight in, answer lands in pF range for cm-scale plates.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The energy density of the electric field in vacuum is given by
questions.explanation: Energy stored per unit volume in an electric field is $u = \dfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2$.
questions.trick: Energy density formula: $\frac12\varepsilon_0E^2$ — same $\frac12$ pattern as $\frac12CV^2$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Two capacitors of 2 $\mu$F and 2 $\mu$F are connected in series, and this combination is connected in parallel with a third capacitor of 3 $\mu$F. The equivalent capacitance is
questions.explanation: Series combination of the two 2 $\mu$F capacitors gives $1\,\mu$F; this in parallel with 3 $\mu$F gives $1+3=4\,\mu$F.
questions.trick: Reduce series pairs first to a single value, then add parallel branches.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A parallel plate capacitor of capacitance 5 pF (with air) is completely filled with a dielectric of dielectric constant 6. Its new capacitance is
questions.explanation: $C' = KC = 6\times5 = 30$ pF.
questions.trick: $C'=KC$ — dielectric constant is a direct multiplier on capacitance.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: In a Van de Graaff generator, charge sprayed onto the inside of a large hollow conducting sphere
options: remains uniformly distributed inside the volume
stays on the inner surface near the point of spraying
immediately moves to the outer surface of the sphere
questions.explanation: Charge given to a hollow conductor always moves to its outer surface, allowing the sphere's potential to keep rising as more charge is added.
questions.trick: Hollow conductor: sprayed charge always migrates entirely to the outer surface.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Two capacitors of 4 $\mu$F and 6 $\mu$F are connected in parallel across a 10 V battery. The total energy stored is
questions.explanation: $C_{eq} = 10\,\mu$F; $U = \dfrac12CV^2 = \dfrac12\times10\times10^{-6}\times100 = 500\,\mu$J.
questions.trick: Parallel: capacitances add first, then use $U=\frac12C_{eq}V^2$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The electric potential at a point 20 cm from a point charge of 4 $\mu$C is
questions.explanation: $V = kq/r = 9\times10^9\times4\times10^{-6}/0.2 = 1.8\times10^5$ V.
questions.trick: $V=kq/r$ — potential is scalar, just divide, no direction needed.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: An isolated charged capacitor (battery disconnected) has a dielectric slab of dielectric constant 4 inserted between its plates. The energy stored
questions.explanation: With charge $Q$ fixed, $C$ becomes $4C$, so $U = Q^2/2C$ decreases to $U/4$.
questions.trick: Isolated capacitor → $Q$ fixed, $C\to KC$, so $U=Q^2/2C$ falls by factor $K$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A parallel plate capacitor with air as dielectric has capacitance $C$. If the separation between plates is halved and a dielectric of constant $K=4$ completely fills the gap, the new capacitance is
questions.explanation: $C \propto K/d$. Halving $d$ doubles $C$; inserting $K=4$ multiplies by 4: net factor $= 2\times4 = 8$, so $C' = 8C$.
questions.trick: $C\propto K/d$: multiply the separate factors (halved $d$ $\times2$, $K=4$ $\times4$) $=8C$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Four equal charges of $+1\,\mu$C each are placed at the four corners of a square such that each corner is 10 cm from the centre. The electric potential at the centre is
questions.explanation: Potential is scalar: $V=4\times\dfrac{kq}{r}=4\times\dfrac{9\times10^9\times10^{-6}}{0.1}=4\times9\times10^4=3.6\times10^5$ V.
questions.trick: Potential is scalar: just multiply single-charge $V$ by the number of identical charges.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: For a system of three point charges $q_1, q_2, q_3$ at mutual separations $r_{12}, r_{13}, r_{23}$, the total electrostatic potential energy of the system is
questions.explanation: The total potential energy is the sum of the pairwise potential energies over all pairs of charges.
questions.trick: Total PE of a charge system = sum over ALL distinct pairs, not just one.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The work done in moving a charge along a closed path in an electrostatic field is always
questions.explanation: The electrostatic field is conservative, so the net work done around any closed path is always zero.
questions.trick: Conservative field → net work round any closed loop is always zero.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The dielectric constant $K$ of a medium is defined as the ratio of
options: electric field in vacuum to permittivity of the medium
capacitance with dielectric to capacitance without dielectric (vacuum), for the same capacitor
capacitance without dielectric to capacitance with dielectric, for the same capacitor
charge to voltage ratio in vacuum
questions.explanation: Dielectric constant $K=C_{medium}/C_{vacuum}$ for the same capacitor geometry; it is always $\ge1$.
questions.trick: $K=C_{medium}/C_{vacuum}$, always $\ge1$ — dielectric increases capacitance.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: $n$ identical capacitors, each of capacitance $C$, connected in series give an equivalent capacitance of
questions.explanation: In series, $1/C_{eq}=n/C \Rightarrow C_{eq}=C/n$.
questions.trick: $n$ identical in series: $C_{eq}=C/n$ — divide by count.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The work done in moving a charge along an equipotential surface is
questions.explanation: All points on an equipotential surface are at the same potential, so $W=q(V_A-V_B)=0$.
questions.trick: Equipotential surface → same $V$ everywhere → work done is always zero.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A capacitor of 4 $\mu$F is charged to a potential difference of 50 V and then disconnected and connected in parallel to an uncharged 4 $\mu$F capacitor. The common potential is
questions.explanation: Charge is conserved: $Q = 4\times50 = 200\,\mu$C shared over total capacitance $8\,\mu$F; $V = 200/8 = 25$ V.
questions.trick: Charge conserves on parallel connection: total $Q$ over total $C$ gives common $V$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A 100 W, 220 V bulb has a resistance of
questions.trick: Bulb resistance: $R=V_{rated}^2/P_{rated}$ — always use rated values, not actual.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The electromotive force (emf) of a cell is defined as the
options: work done per unit charge by the source in driving charge around the complete circuit, including through the cell itself
resistance offered by the cell to current flow
maximum current the cell can supply
potential difference across its terminals when maximum current flows
questions.explanation: EMF is the total work done per unit charge by the source in moving charge around the entire circuit; it equals the terminal voltage only when no current flows (open circuit).
questions.trick: EMF = work per unit charge round the WHOLE circuit, including inside the cell.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The SI unit of mobility of charge carriers is
questions.trick: Mobility unit: $v_d/E$ = (m/s)/(V/m) = m$^2$V$^{-1}$s$^{-1}$, build it from definition.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: In a semiconductor, $5\times10^{18}$ electrons per second cross a section moving to the left while $5\times10^{18}$ holes per second cross the same section moving to the right (e $=1.6\times10^{-19}$ C). The resulting current is
questions.explanation: Electrons moving left give a conventional current of $I=ne=5\times10^{18}\times1.6\times10^{-19}=0.8$ A to the right; holes moving right also give 0.8 A to the right. Since both currents point the same way, they add: total $=1.6$ A.
questions.trick: Electrons left + holes right both push conventional current the same way, add them.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Two bulbs of 60 W and 100 W (both rated 220 V) are connected in series to a 220 V supply. Then
questions.explanation: In series the same current flows; power $= I^2R$. The 60 W bulb has higher resistance ($V^2/P$), so it dissipates more power and glows brighter.
questions.trick: Series circuit: LOWER wattage bulb has higher R, so it glows brighter.
questions.tip: Series → higher resistance (lower wattage) bulb brighter. Parallel → higher wattage brighter.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Resistors of 2 $\Omega$, 3 $\Omega$ and 5 $\Omega$ are connected in series and carry the same current for the same time. The ratio of heat produced in them is
questions.explanation: Heat $H=I^2Rt$. With the same $I$ and $t$, $H\propto R$, so the ratio is simply $2:3:5$.
questions.trick: Series, same current: heat ratio equals resistance ratio directly.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The current flowing through a wire decreases linearly from 8 A to zero in 4 s. The total charge that flows through the wire in this interval is
questions.explanation: Charge equals the area under the I-t graph. For a straight line from 8 A to 0 over 4 s, this area is a triangle: $q=\dfrac12\times4\times8=16$ C.
questions.trick: Charge = area under I-t graph; for a straight-line drop, it's a triangle.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A 4 $\Omega$ resistor is connected in series with a parallel combination of 6 $\Omega$ and 3 $\Omega$ resistors. The total resistance of the combination is
questions.explanation: Parallel: $\dfrac{6\times3}{6+3}=2\,\Omega$; in series with 4 $\Omega$: total $=4+2=6\,\Omega$.
questions.trick: Solve the parallel branch first, then simply add the series resistor.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Current density $J$ at a point in a conductor is defined as
options: current per unit area of cross-section, in the direction of current flow
questions.explanation: Current density is a vector, $J=I/A$, representing current flowing per unit cross-sectional area in the direction of current flow.
questions.trick: Current density $J=I/A$ is a vector along current flow — not per length or volume.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Three wires of the same material have masses in the ratio 1:2:3 and lengths in the ratio 3:2:1. The ratio of their resistances $R_1:R_2:R_3$ is
questions.explanation: Since volume $=m/d$ is fixed for a given mass, $A=m/(dl)$, so $R=\rho l/A=\rho d\,l^2/m$, i.e. $R\propto l^2/m$. Using the ratios: $R_1:R_2:R_3=\dfrac{9}{1}:\dfrac{4}{2}:\dfrac{1}{3}=9:2:\dfrac13=27:6:1$.
questions.trick: Same-material wires: $R\propto l^2/m$, combine length-squared and mass ratios.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: In a metre bridge experiment, the resistance wire AB is replaced by another uniform wire of the same material and length but twice the radius. The balancing length for the same two resistances in the gaps
questions.explanation: The balance condition $R/X=l/(100-l)$ depends only on the ratio of the two wire-segment resistances, which equals the ratio of their lengths since both segments have identical cross-section and material. Changing the wire's radius scales both segments' resistance equally, so the balancing length is unaffected.
questions.trick: Metre bridge balance depends only on the LENGTH ratio, not the wire's radius.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A bulb is rated 220 V, 100 W. If the supply voltage drops by 4% of its rated value, the percentage decrease in the power consumed is approximately
questions.explanation: Since $P=V^2/R$, for small changes $\dfrac{\Delta P}{P}\approx2\dfrac{\Delta V}{V}=2\times4\%=8\%$.
questions.trick: $P\propto V^2$: percentage change in $P$ is about double the percentage change in $V$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Two identical cells, each of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 1 $\Omega$, are connected in parallel across an external resistance of 2 $\Omega$. The current through the external resistance is
questions.explanation: For $m$ identical cells in parallel, $I=\dfrac{E}{R+r/m}=\dfrac{1.5}{2+0.5}=0.6$ A.
questions.trick: Identical cells in parallel: use $I=E/(R+r/m)$ with $m$ = number of cells.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: $n$ identical cells, each of emf $E$ and internal resistance $r$, are connected in series across an external resistance $R$. The current is
questions.explanation: Total emf $nE$, total internal resistance $nr$: $I = \dfrac{nE}{R+nr}$.
questions.trick: $n$ cells in series: emf and internal resistance both scale by $n$: $nE/(R+nr)$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: An ideal ammeter should have
options: resistance equal to the galvanometer resistance
resistance equal to the circuit resistance
questions.explanation: An ideal ammeter, connected in series, should have zero resistance so that it does not alter the current it is measuring.
questions.trick: Ideal ammeter: zero resistance (in series, shouldn't add resistance).
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: An ideal voltmeter should have
options: resistance equal to that of the component across which it is connected
questions.explanation: An ideal voltmeter, connected in parallel, should have infinite resistance so that it draws no current and does not change the potential difference being measured.
questions.trick: Ideal voltmeter: infinite resistance (in parallel, shouldn't draw current).
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: An electrical appliance rated 2000 W is used for 3 hours daily. The energy consumed in 5 days, in kWh, is
questions.explanation: Energy $= P\times t = 2\,\text{kW}\times3\,\text{h}\times5\,\text{days} = 30$ kWh.
questions.trick: Energy = power(kW) $\times$ hours/day $\times$ days — straight multiplication, keep units in kWh.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A copper wire is drawn thinner (its cross-sectional area is reduced) while its length is kept fixed. The resistivity of the copper
options: remains unchanged, since it depends only on the material and temperature
questions.explanation: Resistivity is a material property (depending only on the material and temperature), unaffected by changes in the conductor's dimensions; only the resistance $R=\rho l/A$ changes.
questions.trick: Resistivity is material-only — changing wire dimensions changes $R$, never $\rho$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: In a balanced Wheatstone bridge, $P = 2\,\Omega$, $Q = 4\,\Omega$ and $R = 3\,\Omega$. The value of $S$ is
questions.explanation: $P/Q = R/S \Rightarrow S = QR/P = 4\times3/2 = 6\,\Omega$.
questions.trick: Wheatstone balance: cross-multiply $P/Q=R/S$, solve for the unknown arm.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: In a potentiometer experiment, the balancing length for a cell is 240 cm on open circuit. When a 2 $\Omega$ resistor is connected across the cell, the balancing length becomes 120 cm. The internal resistance of the cell is
questions.explanation: $r = R\left(\dfrac{l_1}{l_2} - 1\right) = 2\left(\dfrac{240}{120} - 1\right) = 2\,\Omega$.
questions.trick: $r=R(l_1/l_2-1)$ — plug open-circuit and loaded balancing lengths directly.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A carbon resistor has colour bands red, violet, orange, gold. Its resistance is
questions.explanation: Red = 2, violet = 7, orange = $10^3$ → $27\times10^3 = 27$ k$\Omega$; gold = ±5%.
questions.trick: Colour code: 1st-2nd digits, 3rd=multiplier power of 10, 4th=tolerance.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The SI unit of electrical conductivity is
questions.explanation: Conductivity $\sigma=1/\rho$ has SI unit siemens per metre (S/m), the reciprocal of resistivity's unit ($\Omega$ m).
questions.trick: Conductivity unit is S/m — reciprocal of resistivity's $\Omega\cdot$m, invert to recall.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Kirchhoff's junction rule is a consequence of conservation of
questions.explanation: Charge cannot accumulate at a junction, so the total current in equals the total current out. The loop rule follows from conservation of energy.
questions.trick: Junction rule = charge conservation; loop rule = energy conservation — don't swap them.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A galvanometer of resistance 100 $\Omega$ gives full-scale deflection for a current of 1 mA. To convert it into a voltmeter of range 10 V, the resistance that must be connected in series with it is
questions.explanation: Series resistance $R=\dfrac{V}{I_g}-G=\dfrac{10}{0.001}-100=10000-100=9900\,\Omega$.
questions.trick: Voltmeter series resistor: $R=V/I_g-G$, subtract galvanometer resistance at the end.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Maximum power is delivered by a cell of internal resistance $r$ to an external resistance $R$ when
questions.explanation: $P = \dfrac{E^2R}{(R+r)^2}$ is maximum when $R = r$ (maximum power transfer theorem); then $P_{max} = E^2/4r$.
questions.trick: Max power transfer: always $R=r$, giving $P_{max}=E^2/4r$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The resistance of a conductor is 5 $\Omega$ at 50°C and 6 $\Omega$ at 100°C. Its resistance at 0°C is
questions.explanation: $R = R_0(1+\alpha t)$: $5 = R_0(1+50\alpha)$, $6 = R_0(1+100\alpha)$. Dividing: $6(1+50\alpha) = 5(1+100\alpha) \Rightarrow 1 = 200\alpha \Rightarrow \alpha = 1/200$. Then $R_0 = 5/(1+0.25) = 4\,\Omega$.
questions.trick: Two $R$-$t$ equations, $R=R_0(1+\alpha t)$: solve simultaneously for $\alpha$ then $R_0$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: In a balanced Wheatstone bridge with arms $P$, $Q$, $R$, $S$, the resistance of every arm is doubled. The bridge
options: shows a large deflection in the galvanometer
questions.explanation: The balance condition is $P/Q=R/S$. Doubling every arm gives $2P/2Q=P/Q$ and $2R/2S=R/S$, so the ratios, and hence the balance, are unaffected.
questions.trick: Scaling all four Wheatstone arms equally never disturbs the $P/Q=R/S$ balance.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: In a circuit, a 2 $\Omega$ resistor is in series with a parallel combination of 3 $\Omega$ and 6 $\Omega$ resistors, connected to a 12 V battery of negligible internal resistance. The current through the 6 $\Omega$ resistor is
questions.explanation: Parallel part: $\dfrac{3\times6}{3+6}=2\,\Omega$; total resistance $=2+2=4\,\Omega$; total current $=12/4=3$ A; voltage across parallel part $=3\times2=6$ V; current through 6 $\Omega$ $=6/6=1$ A.
questions.trick: Reduce parallel branch, find total current, then back-calculate voltage across it for branch currents.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A cell of emf $E$ and internal resistance $r$ is short-circuited (external resistance = 0). The current drawn from the cell is
questions.explanation: With $R=0$, $I=E/(R+r)=E/r$, the maximum current the cell can deliver.
questions.trick: Short circuit ($R=0$): current is simply $E/r$, the cell's maximum output.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A cell of emf 2 V and internal resistance 1 $\Omega$ is connected to an external resistance of 4 $\Omega$. The terminal voltage of the cell is
questions.trick: Terminal V $=IR$, computed from $I=E/(R+r)$ — quicker than $E-Ir$ here.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The sensitivity of a potentiometer (its ability to measure small potential differences) can be increased by
options: decreasing the potential gradient along the wire (e.g. using a longer wire)
increasing the potential gradient along the wire
increasing the current through the wire
decreasing the length of the potentiometer wire
questions.explanation: A smaller potential gradient ($E$ per unit length) means a larger balancing length for a given potential difference, allowing finer (more sensitive) measurement; this is achieved with a longer wire.
questions.trick: Lower potential gradient (longer wire) = higher potentiometer sensitivity.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Four identical cells, each of emf 2 V and internal resistance 0.25 $\Omega$, are connected in series, but one cell is connected with reversed polarity. This combination is joined to an external resistance of 4 $\Omega$. The current in the circuit is
questions.explanation: One reversed cell cancels itself and opposes one correct cell, so net emf $=(4-2)\times2=4$ V. Internal resistances still add regardless of polarity: total $r=4\times0.25=1\,\Omega$. Current $=\dfrac{4}{4+1}=0.8$ A.
questions.trick: One reversed cell among $n$: net emf $=(n-2)E$, but total internal resistance still $=nr$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A rectangular current loop of magnetic moment $m$ is placed with its plane parallel to a uniform magnetic field $B$. The torque on the loop is
questions.explanation: When the loop's plane is parallel to $B$, its normal (and $\vec m$) is perpendicular to $B$, so $\theta=90^\circ$: $\tau = mB\sin90^\circ = mB$, the maximum value.
questions.trick: Plane parallel to $B$ means $\vec m\perp\vec B$: torque is maximum, $\tau=mB$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: In a moving coil galvanometer, the magnetic field is made radial (using concave pole pieces and a soft iron cylindrical core) so that
options: the plane of the coil is always parallel to the field, making the torque proportional to current at every deflection (linear scale)
questions.explanation: A radial field keeps the coil's plane always parallel to $B$ ($\theta=90^\circ$ throughout), so $\tau=NIAB$ stays proportional to $I$ at every deflection, giving a linear (uniform) scale.
questions.trick: Radial field keeps coil plane parallel to $B$ always → linear (uniform) scale.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: In a cyclotron, a charged particle gains kinetic energy $qV$ each time it crosses the gap between the dees, where $V$ is the accelerating voltage. Since it crosses the gap twice per revolution, the energy gained per revolution is
questions.explanation: The particle is accelerated once in each half of a revolution (twice per full revolution), gaining $qV$ each time, for a total of $2qV$ per revolution.
questions.trick: Two accelerations per revolution (once per dee gap): total energy gain $=2qV$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer can be increased by
options: decreasing the area of the coil
increasing the torsional constant of the spring
increasing the magnetic field and number of turns, and decreasing the torsional constant
questions.explanation: Current sensitivity $= NAB/k$; it increases with more turns $N$, larger area $A$, stronger field $B$, and a smaller torsional constant $k$.
questions.trick: Sensitivity $=NAB/k$: more turns/area/field, weaker spring, all raise sensitivity.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The magnetic field at the centre of a circular current loop of radius $R$ is $B_0$. The field on the axis of the same loop, at a distance $x=R$ from the centre, is
questions.trick: At $x=R$ on axis, field drops to $B_0/2^{3/2}\approx0.354B_0$ — a value worth remembering.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A closed current loop of arbitrary shape is placed in a uniform magnetic field. The net force on the loop is
options: zero, though it may experience a net torque
equal to $BIL$, where $L$ is the loop's perimeter
questions.explanation: In a uniform field, the forces on different current elements of a closed loop sum to zero net force, although a net torque can still act unless the loop's plane is perpendicular to the field.
questions.trick: Uniform field on a closed loop: net force is always zero, torque may still exist.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The period of revolution of a charged particle in a cyclotron
questions.explanation: $T = 2\pi m/(qB)$ has no $v$ or $r$ dependence, which is why a fixed-frequency oscillator can accelerate the particle throughout.
questions.trick: Cyclotron period $T=2\pi m/qB$ has no $v$ — always independent of speed.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: One ampere is defined as the current which, when flowing through each of two long parallel wires kept 1 m apart in vacuum, produces a force per unit length between them of
questions.explanation: Using $F/l=\mu_0I_1I_2/(2\pi d)$ with $I_1=I_2=1$ A and $d=1$ m gives $F/l=2\times10^{-7}$ N/m, which defines the ampere.
questions.trick: Ampere's definition: $2\times10^{-7}$ N/m per amp-pair at 1 m — the defining number.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The magnetic field at the centre of a circular coil of radius 10 cm carrying a current of 5 A, having 20 turns, is
questions.trick: $B=\mu_0NI/2R$ at coil centre — multiply by turns, don't forget.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: To convert a galvanometer of resistance 50 $\Omega$ and full-scale current 2 mA into a voltmeter of range 10 V, the series resistance needed is
questions.trick: Series resistance $R=V/I_g-G$ — always much bigger than $G$ for voltmeter conversion.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: According to the Biot-Savart law, the magnitude of the magnetic field $dB$ due to a current element $Idl$ at a point, making angle $\theta$ with the line joining them, at distance $r$, is proportional to
questions.explanation: The Biot-Savart law gives $dB\propto\dfrac{Idl\sin\theta}{r^2}$, forming the basis for calculating fields due to current distributions.
questions.trick: Biot-Savart: $dB\propto Idl\sin\theta/r^2$ — same $\sin\theta$ pattern as force law.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A charged particle enters a magnetic field with velocity making an angle $\theta$ (not 0 or 90) with $\vec{B}$. Its path is
questions.explanation: The velocity component along $B$ is unaffected (uniform motion) while the perpendicular component causes circular motion; combined, the path is a helix.
questions.trick: Velocity at an angle (not 0/90) to $B$ → path is always a helix.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A solenoid of length $l$ has $N$ turns and carries current $I$, producing a magnetic field $B$ inside it. If the number of turns is doubled (keeping the length and current the same), the new magnetic field is
questions.explanation: $B=\mu_0nI$ with $n=N/l$; doubling $N$ (at fixed $l$) doubles $n$ and hence $B$.
questions.trick: $B=\mu_0nI$, $n=N/l$: doubling turns (fixed length) directly doubles $B$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Two long straight parallel wires, 20 cm apart, carry equal currents in the same direction. The magnetic field exactly midway between them (due to both wires) is
options: twice that due to one wire alone
equal to that due to one wire alone
questions.explanation: Between the wires, the fields due to the two equal, same-direction currents point in opposite directions (by the right-hand rule); being equidistant, they are equal in magnitude at the midpoint and exactly cancel.
questions.trick: Same-direction wires: fields between them point opposite ways and cancel at the midpoint.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The SI unit of magnetic field (magnetic flux density) is
questions.explanation: The SI unit of $B$ is the tesla (T), equal to Wb/m$^2$; gauss is a CGS unit ($1\,\text{T}=10^4$ G).
questions.trick: SI unit of $B$ is tesla; gauss is CGS ($1\,T=10^4\,G$) — don't confuse.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The cyclotron is not suitable for accelerating electrons to high energies mainly because
options: electrons cannot move in a magnetic field
the magnetic field cannot act on electrons
electrons quickly attain relativistic speeds, so their mass increases and they fall out of resonance with the fixed-frequency oscillator
questions.explanation: Because of their small mass, electrons quickly reach speeds where relativistic mass increase becomes significant, changing their cyclotron frequency and desynchronising them from the fixed oscillator frequency.
questions.trick: Electrons fail in cyclotrons: light mass → quickly relativistic → falls out of sync with fixed frequency.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A straight wire of length 0.5 m carrying a current of 4 A is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T, perpendicular to the field. The force on the wire is
questions.explanation: $F = BIl = 0.2\times4\times0.5 = 0.4$ N.
questions.trick: $F=BIl$ — perpendicular case, no $\sin\theta$ factor needed.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A proton (charge $1.6\times10^{-19}$ C, mass $1.6\times10^{-27}$ kg) moves in a cyclotron in a magnetic field of 0.5 T. Its cyclotron frequency is approximately
questions.explanation: $f=\dfrac{qB}{2\pi m}=\dfrac{1.6\times10^{-19}\times0.5}{2\pi\times1.6\times10^{-27}}\approx8\times10^6$ Hz.
questions.trick: Cyclotron frequency $f=qB/2\pi m$ — plug numbers directly, mass cancels the $2\pi$ shape.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The magnetic field outside an ideal toroid, in the space surrounding it, is
questions.explanation: The winding confines the field entirely within the toroid's core; an Amperian loop drawn outside encloses zero net current, so $B=0$ outside an ideal toroid.
questions.trick: Ideal toroid: all field is confined inside the core — zero outside, always.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A proton and an alpha particle, having the same speed, enter a uniform magnetic field perpendicular to their velocity. Given that the alpha particle has 4 times the mass and 2 times the charge of the proton, the ratio of the radius of the proton's circular path to that of the alpha particle's is
questions.explanation: $r=mv/(qB)$. $r_p=\dfrac{m v}{qB}$, $r_\alpha=\dfrac{4m\,v}{2qB}=\dfrac{2mv}{qB}=2r_p$. So $r_p:r_\alpha=1:2$.
questions.trick: $r\propto m/q$: compute the mass/charge ratio for each particle, then compare directly.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A charged particle moves with velocity $v$ perpendicular to a magnetic field $B$. The magnetic force on it is used to provide centripetal force. The radius of its circular path is
questions.explanation: $qvB = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} \Rightarrow r = \dfrac{mv}{qB}$.
questions.trick: $qvB=mv^2/r$ gives $r=mv/qB$ — memorise this one formula cold.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A bar magnet of length 5 cm and magnetic moment 1 A m$^2$ is placed with its axis along an external field of 0.2 T. The work done to rotate it by $90^\circ$ from this position is
questions.explanation: $W = U(90^\circ)-U(0^\circ) = -mB\cos90^\circ-(-mB\cos0^\circ) = 0+mB = 1\times0.2 = 0.2$ J.
questions.trick: Rotating from $0^\circ$ (aligned) to $90^\circ$: work done is simply $mB$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A circular coil of 100 turns and radius 10 cm carries a current of 0.5 A. Its magnetic moment is approximately
questions.explanation: $m = NI\pi r^2 = 100\times0.5\times\pi\times(0.1)^2 = 50\times0.0314 = 1.57$ A m$^2$.
questions.trick: $m=NI\pi r^2$ — treat coil as current loop, use $\pi r^2$ for area.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: In a tangent galvanometer experiment, the horizontal component of Earth's field is balanced against the field due to current in the coil. If the deflection is $\theta$, the relation used is
