questions.explanation: The needle settles along the resultant of the coil's field $B$ (perpendicular to $B_H$) and $B_H$ itself, so $\tan\theta = B/B_H$, giving $B=B_H\tan\theta$ (tangent law).
questions.trick: Tangent law: $B=B_H\tan\theta$ — coil field is perpendicular to $B_H$ by design.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Above the Curie temperature, a ferromagnetic material becomes
questions.explanation: Thermal agitation destroys the domain alignment above the Curie point, and the material behaves as an ordinary paramagnet.
questions.trick: Above Curie point, ferromagnetic $\to$ paramagnetic, always — domains break down.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: If the horizontal component of Earth's field at a place is 0.24 G and the angle of dip is such that $\tan\delta = 1.5$, the vertical component is
questions.explanation: $B_V = B_H\tan\delta = 0.24\times1.5 = 0.36$ G.
questions.trick: $B_V=B_H\tan\delta$ — direct multiplication, no need for $B$ itself.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The magnetic dipole moment of a bar magnet of pole strength 5 A m and length 10 cm is
questions.explanation: $m = q_m\times2l = 5\times0.1 = 0.5$ A m$^2$.
questions.trick: $m=q_m\times2l$ — plug pole strength and full length directly.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A bar magnet of magnetic moment $m$ and length $2l$ is cut into two equal pieces by a cut perpendicular to its length. The magnetic moment of each piece is
questions.explanation: Each piece has the same pole strength $q_m$ but half the length ($l$ instead of $2l$), so its moment is $q_m l = m/2$.
questions.trick: Cut perpendicular to length: pole strength unchanged, length halves, so $m\to m/2$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: At a place, the angle of dip is $45^\circ$. If the horizontal component of Earth's magnetic field is $0.3$ G, the vertical component is
questions.explanation: $\tan\delta = B_V/B_H \Rightarrow B_V = B_H\tan45^\circ = 0.3\times1 = 0.3$ G.
questions.trick: $\tan45^\circ=1$, so $B_V=B_H$ — a freebie whenever dip is $45^\circ$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Compared to soft iron, the hysteresis loop of steel is
options: absent, since steel shows no hysteresis
fatter, with larger retentivity and coercivity, hence larger hysteresis loss
questions.explanation: Steel has high retentivity and coercivity (good for permanent magnets) but this means a fatter loop and greater hysteresis loss compared to soft iron, which has a thin loop suited to electromagnets.
questions.trick: Fatter hysteresis loop = more retentivity/coercivity = more loss — that's steel vs soft iron.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Which pair correctly matches material type with susceptibility sign?
questions.explanation: Paramagnetic materials have small positive $\chi$ (weakly attracted); diamagnetic materials have small negative $\chi$ (weakly repelled).
questions.trick: Sign rule: paramagnetic $\chi>0$ (attracted), diamagnetic $\chi<0$ (repelled).
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Inside a bar magnet, the magnetic field lines run from
options: there are no field lines inside a magnet
N pole to S pole, same as outside
S pole to N pole, forming closed loops with the external field lines
questions.explanation: Magnetic field lines have no beginning or end; outside a magnet they go from N to S, and inside they continue from S back to N, forming closed loops (consistent with $\oint\vec B\cdot d\vec A=0$).
questions.trick: Field lines inside a magnet go S to N, closing the loop with outside N to S.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A bar magnet is dropped, north pole down, through a horizontal conducting loop. As the magnet approaches the loop from above, the induced current in the loop (viewed from above) is
options: clockwise, to oppose the increasing downward flux
clockwise, to aid the flux increase
anticlockwise, to oppose the increasing downward flux
questions.explanation: As the magnet approaches, downward flux through the loop increases; by Lenz's law the induced current flows anticlockwise (viewed from above the falling magnet's side) to create an opposing upward field.
questions.trick: Approaching magnet increases flux; induced current always opposes — apply Lenz's law, then right-hand rule.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A bar magnet and a coil approach each other with the same relative speed in two situations: (i) magnet fixed, coil moves; (ii) coil fixed, magnet moves. The induced emf in the coil is
options: the same in both cases, depending only on relative velocity
questions.explanation: Since only the relative motion between magnet and coil determines the rate of change of flux, the induced emf is identical in both cases for the same relative speed.
questions.trick: Only relative velocity between magnet and coil matters — emf is the same either way.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A metal rod of length $l=1$ m slides at constant velocity $v=2$ m/s on resistance-free rails (total circuit resistance $R=2\,\Omega$) in a uniform magnetic field $B=0.5$ T perpendicular to the plane of the rails. The power delivered by the external agent to keep the rod moving at this constant velocity is
questions.explanation: $P = F v = (B^2l^2v/R)\times v = B^2l^2v^2/R = 0.25\times1\times4/2 = 0.5$ W, equal to $I^2R$ dissipated.
questions.trick: Power by external agent = power dissipated = $B^2l^2v^2/R$ — extra factor of $v$ over force.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The electric field induced by a time-varying magnetic field differs from an electrostatic field in that it
options: has closed field lines and is non-conservative
questions.explanation: An induced electric field forms closed loops around the region of changing flux and does non-zero work around a closed path, unlike the conservative, radial electrostatic field of charges.
questions.trick: Induced E-field forms closed loops (non-conservative) — unlike electrostatic field's open radial lines.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: As an electric motor speeds up, the back emf generated in its armature
options: decreases, increasing the net current drawn
has no effect on the current
increases, reducing the net current drawn from the supply
questions.explanation: The rotating armature coil generates a back emf $\varepsilon_b$ opposing the applied voltage; as speed increases $\varepsilon_b$ increases, so the net current $i=(V-\varepsilon_b)/R$ decreases.
questions.trick: Back emf rises with motor speed, always REDUCING net current drawn — self-regulating mechanism.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Eddy currents in a transformer core are minimised by
options: using a laminated core of thin insulated sheets
using a hollow core with no material
questions.explanation: Laminating the core into thin sheets insulated from each other increases resistance to eddy current paths, reducing eddy current (heating) losses without affecting the main flux.
questions.trick: Laminating the core (thin insulated sheets) is THE standard fix for eddy current loss.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The coefficient of coupling $k$ between two coils is defined as $k = M/\sqrt{L_1L_2}$. Its value lies in the range
questions.explanation: $k=0$ means no flux linkage between coils; $k=1$ means perfect coupling (no leakage flux); $k$ cannot exceed 1.
questions.trick: Coupling coefficient $k$ always lies between 0 (no linkage) and 1 (perfect coupling).
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction is applicable to
options: only a changing magnetic field with the conductor at rest
both motional emf and emf due to a changing field with the coil at rest
questions.explanation: Faraday's law, $\varepsilon=-Nd\phi/dt$, is completely general — it covers emf from a conductor moving through a field as well as emf from a purely time-varying field with a stationary coil.
questions.trick: Faraday's law covers BOTH motional emf and changing-field emf — fully general, no restriction.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Two coils have a mutual inductance of 0.5 H. If the current in the primary changes at the rate of 4 A/s, the emf induced in the secondary is
questions.explanation: $\varepsilon_2 = M\dfrac{dI_1}{dt} = 0.5\times4 = 2$ V.
questions.trick: $\varepsilon_2=M\,dI_1/dt$ — direct multiplication, ignore turns in secondary explicitly.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The energy stored in an inductor of 2 H carrying a current of 5 A is
questions.explanation: $U = \dfrac12LI^2 = \dfrac12\times2\times25 = 25$ J.
questions.trick: $U=\frac12LI^2$ — same $\frac12$ pattern as capacitor and kinetic energy.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The direction of induced current in a circuit is given by
questions.explanation: Lenz's law specifies the direction: the induced current opposes the change in flux causing it.
questions.trick: Direction of induced current = Lenz's law; magnitude = Faraday's law — know which does what.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: For a series RL ac circuit with $R=40\,\Omega$ and $X_L=30\,\Omega$ (so $Z=50\,\Omega$), the power factor is
questions.trick: Power factor $=R/Z$ always — the resistive fraction of total impedance.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: An ac source of rms voltage 100 V is connected in series with a resistor $R=30\,\Omega$ and a capacitor with $X_C=40\,\Omega$. The rms current in the circuit is
questions.trick: RC circuit: $Z=\sqrt{R^2+X_C^2}$, same Pythagoras pattern as RL, just swap $X_L$ for $X_C$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: In a purely inductive ac circuit, the current
questions.explanation: For an inductor, $V=L\,di/dt$ makes the current lag the voltage by $90^\circ$ ('ELI').
questions.trick: Remember 'ELI': in an inductor, EMF leads current — current LAGS by 90°.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A transformer has an input power of 2000 W. If the total power loss (copper + iron losses) is 100 W, its efficiency is
questions.explanation: Efficiency $=\dfrac{\text{output}}{\text{input}}\times100=\dfrac{2000-100}{2000}\times100=95\%$.
questions.trick: Transformer efficiency $=(\text{input}-\text{loss})/\text{input}\times100$ — subtract loss from input first.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: At resonance in a series LCR circuit with a high Q-factor, the voltage across the inductor (or capacitor) compared to the applied source voltage is
options: much larger than the source voltage (voltage magnification by factor $Q$)
always less than the source voltage
always equal to the source voltage
questions.explanation: At resonance, $V_L=V_C=Q\times V_{source}$; a high-$Q$ circuit can develop voltages across $L$ and $C$ far exceeding the applied voltage, even though they cancel in the total impedance.
questions.trick: At resonance, $V_L=V_C=Q\times V_{source}$ — high Q means voltage magnification across L, C.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The rms value of the mains ac supply is 220 V. Its peak value is approximately
questions.explanation: $V_0=V_{rms}\times\sqrt2=220\times1.414\approx311$ V.
questions.trick: $V_0=V_{rms}\times\sqrt2$ — for 220 V mains this gives the classic 311 V peak.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: In a series LCR circuit at resonance, the power factor is
questions.explanation: At resonance the circuit is purely resistive ($\phi=0$), so $\cos\phi = 1$.
questions.trick: At resonance power factor is always exactly 1 — purely resistive behaviour.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: At resonance, a parallel LC circuit (tank circuit) has
options: maximum impedance and minimum line current (current magnification in the branches)
impedance independent of L and C
minimum impedance and maximum line current
questions.explanation: Unlike series resonance, a parallel LCR/LC circuit at resonance offers maximum impedance to the source, so the line current drawn is minimum, even though large circulating currents exist in the L and C branches.
questions.trick: Parallel LC (tank) at resonance: impedance is MAXIMUM, current MINIMUM — opposite of series.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: An LC circuit has $L=0.01$ H and $C=1\,\mu$F. Its natural angular frequency of oscillation is
questions.trick: $\omega=1/\sqrt{LC}$ — same formula whether asked as $f_0$ or $\omega$, watch which is wanted.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: For a series LCR resonant circuit with resonant angular frequency $\omega_0=1000$ rad/s and bandwidth $\Delta\omega=20$ rad/s, the quality factor $Q$ is
questions.explanation: $Q=\omega_0/\Delta\omega=1000/20=50$; a larger $Q$ means a sharper resonance curve.
questions.trick: $Q=\omega_0/\Delta\omega$ — resonant frequency divided by bandwidth, straightforward.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A series LCR circuit has $R=30\,\Omega$, $X_L=70\,\Omega$, $X_C=30\,\Omega$. The impedance of the circuit is
questions.trick: $Z=\sqrt{R^2+(X_L-X_C)^2}$ — subtract reactances first, then Pythagoras.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The resonant frequency of a series LCR circuit with $L=1$ H and $C=1\,\mu$F is nearly
questions.explanation: $f_0 = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{1\times10^{-6}}} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\times10^{-3}} \approx 159$ Hz.
questions.trick: $f_0=1/(2\pi\sqrt{LC})$ — same shape as $\omega_0$, just divide by $2\pi$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Eddy current losses in a transformer core are reduced by
questions.explanation: Laminating the core with thin, mutually insulated sheets restricts the paths available for eddy currents, reducing heating losses.
questions.trick: Eddy current fix in transformers: laminated core, same trick as in motors/generators.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A 100 V, 50 Hz ac source is connected to a series combination of $R=40\,\Omega$ and $X_L=30\,\Omega$ (no capacitor). The current in the circuit is
questions.trick: RL circuit (no C): $Z=\sqrt{R^2+X_L^2}$ then $I=V/Z$ — standard two-step.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: An ac source of rms voltage 220 V is connected to a pure resistor of 100 $\Omega$. The average power dissipated is
questions.trick: Pure resistor: $P=V_{rms}^2/R$, use rms voltage directly, no $\cos\phi$ needed.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The capacitive reactance of a 10 $\mu$F capacitor at 50 Hz is approximately
questions.explanation: $X_C = 1/(2\pi fC) = 1/(2\pi\times50\times10\times10^{-6}) = 1/(3.14\times10^{-3}) \approx 318\,\Omega$.
questions.trick: $X_C=1/(2\pi fC)$ — reciprocal relation, larger $C$ means smaller $X_C$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Gamma rays used in the treatment of cancer are produced by
options: de-excitation of nuclei following radioactive decay
sudden stopping of electrons in an X-ray tube
questions.explanation: Gamma rays originate from nuclear transitions/decays, unlike X-rays which arise from electron transitions or deceleration; this is a common point of confusion in KCET.
questions.trick: Gamma = nuclear origin; X-rays = electron origin. Don't swap them.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The ratio of amplitudes of electric and magnetic fields in an electromagnetic wave in vacuum equals
questions.explanation: $E_0/B_0 = c$, the speed of light, a direct consequence of Maxwell's equations.
questions.trick: $E_0/B_0=c$ always in vacuum — memorise this one ratio.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: An electromagnetic wave travels along the $-y$ direction with its electric field along $+z$. The magnetic field must be along
questions.explanation: Propagation direction is along $\vec E\times\vec B$; with $\vec E$ along $+z$ and propagation along $-y$, $\vec B$ must be along $-x$, since $\hat z\times(-\hat x)=-\hat y$.
questions.trick: Use $\hat E\times\hat B=$ propagation direction; solve via unit-vector cross product.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Displacement current arises due to
options: motion of free electrons in a conductor
questions.explanation: Maxwell defined $I_d = \varepsilon_0\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt}$, which exists wherever the electric flux through a surface changes with time, such as between capacitor plates while charging.
questions.trick: $I_d=\varepsilon_0\dfrac{d\Phi_E}{dt}$: displacement current needs changing E, not steady current itself.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The existence of electromagnetic waves, predicted theoretically by Maxwell, was first experimentally demonstrated by
questions.explanation: Heinrich Hertz generated and detected radio waves in the laboratory in 1887, confirming Maxwell's theoretical prediction of electromagnetic waves.
questions.trick: Maxwell predicted, Hertz proved (1887) — the classic theory-vs-experiment pairing.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The direction of energy flow (and wave propagation) in an electromagnetic wave is given by the direction of
options: the Poynting vector, $\vec S = \vec E \times \vec H$
questions.explanation: The Poynting vector $\vec S=\vec E\times\vec H$ gives both the direction and magnitude of energy flux carried by an electromagnetic wave, and points along the direction of propagation.
questions.trick: Poynting vector $\vec S=\vec E\times\vec H$ points along wave propagation and energy flow.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: For an equilateral prism ($A=60^\circ$), the angle of minimum deviation happens to equal the angle of the prism itself ($\delta_m = A = 60^\circ$). The speed of light inside this prism is
questions.explanation: $n=\dfrac{\sin\frac{A+\delta_m}{2}}{\sin\frac A2}=\dfrac{\sin60^\circ}{\sin30^\circ}=\dfrac{0.866}{0.5}=\sqrt3$. So $v=c/n=3\times10^8/\sqrt3\approx1.73\times10^8$ m/s.
questions.trick: Special case $\delta_m=A$: $n=2\cos(A/2)$ — then find $v=c/n$ directly.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: An ink dot is viewed from directly above through a travelling microscope. When a glass slab of thickness 6 cm is placed over the dot, it appears to rise (shift upward) by 2 cm. The refractive index of the glass is
questions.explanation: Apparent shift $=t\left(1-\dfrac1n\right)$. So $2=6\left(1-\dfrac1n\right) \Rightarrow 1-\dfrac1n=\dfrac13 \Rightarrow \dfrac1n=\dfrac23 \Rightarrow n=1.5$.
questions.trick: Apparent rise through slab: shift $=t(1-1/n)$ — solve for $n$ directly.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A mirage is formed on a hot road because
options: air near the ground is denser (higher $n$) than the air above it, bending light upward
water actually collects on the road surface
hot air near the ground has a lower refractive index than the cooler air above, causing rays from the sky to bend and undergo (near) total internal reflection, appearing as a reflection
light from the sky is reflected by a silvered layer of sand
questions.explanation: Hot air close to the road is less dense (lower $n$) than the cooler air above; light from the sky refracts continuously through these layers and eventually curves upward as if reflected, creating the illusion of a water pool.
questions.trick: Mirage: hot ground air has lower $n$ → light curves up, mimics reflection.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The magnifying power of a simple microscope of focal length 5 cm, when the image is formed at the near point (25 cm), is
questions.trick: Near-point viewing: $m=1+D/f$; at infinity drop the '+1'.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Two thin lenses of powers $+5$ D and $-2$ D are placed in contact. The focal length of the combination is
questions.explanation: $P = 5 - 2 = 3$ D → $f = 1/3$ m $= 33.3$ cm, converging.
questions.trick: Lenses in contact: powers simply add, $P=P_1+P_2$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A symmetric biconvex lens of focal length 15 cm is cut by a plane perpendicular to the principal axis, through its optical centre, giving two plano-convex halves. The focal length of each half is
questions.explanation: Cutting perpendicular to the axis gives each half only one curved surface instead of two, halving its power; since power is halved, the focal length doubles: $2\times15=30$ cm.
questions.trick: Perpendicular cut splits a symmetric biconvex lens into two lenses of focal length $2f$ each.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Optical fibres transmit light over long distances with very little loss using
options: total internal reflection at the core-cladding interface, since the core has a higher refractive index than the cladding
ordinary reflection from a silvered coating
questions.explanation: Light entering the fibre core (higher $n$) strikes the core-cladding boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle and undergoes repeated total internal reflection, travelling with minimal loss.
questions.trick: Optical fibre works via TIR: core $n$ greater than cladding $n$, always.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A plano-convex lens of focal length 20 cm has its plane surface silvered. It now behaves like a mirror of focal length
questions.explanation: For a lens silvered on one face, equivalent power $P_{eq}=2P_{lens}+P_{mirror}$. With the plane face silvered ($P_{mirror}=0$), $P_{eq}=2/20=0.1$, giving $f_{eq}=10$ cm, behaving as a converging (concave-type) mirror.
questions.trick: Silvered lens acts as a mirror: $P_{eq}=2P_{lens}+P_{mirror}$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: An equiconvex lens of glass ($n=1.5$) has a certain focal length in air. When it is completely immersed in water ($n=4/3$), the percentage increase in its focal length is
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{f_w}{f_a}=\dfrac{n_g-1}{n_g/n_w-1}=\dfrac{0.5}{1.125-1}=4$, so the focal length becomes 4 times its original value — an increase of $(4-1)\times100\% = 300\%$.
questions.trick: Lens in water: focal length becomes 4$\times$ for $n=1.5$ glass — a 300% rise.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A ray of light passes symmetrically through an equilateral glass prism (angle of prism $A=60^\circ$) such that the angle of incidence equals the angle of emergence, each equal to $\dfrac34$ of the angle of the prism. The angle of deviation is
questions.explanation: $i=e=\dfrac34\times60^\circ=45^\circ$. Deviation $\delta=i+e-A=45+45-60=30^\circ$.
questions.trick: Prism deviation: $\delta=i+e-A$ — plug in the given $i$ and $e$ directly.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The objective lens of a telescope has a diameter of 10 cm. For light of wavelength 550 nm, the telescope's limit of resolution (minimum resolvable angular separation) is approximately
questions.explanation: Limit of resolution $\Delta\theta = \dfrac{1.22\lambda}{D} = \dfrac{1.22\times550\times10^{-9}}{0.10} \approx 6.7\times10^{-6}$ rad.
questions.trick: Telescope resolving power: $\Delta\theta=1.22\lambda/D$ — smaller angle means finer resolution.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: In an astronomical telescope, decreasing the focal length of the eyepiece
options: has no effect on the magnifying power
increases the magnifying power but reduces the field of view
questions.explanation: $m=f_o/f_e$, so a smaller $f_e$ gives higher magnification, but this comes at the cost of a narrower field of view.
questions.trick: Smaller eyepiece $f_e$ gives more zoom but a narrower field of view — trade-off.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A convex lens of focal length 10 cm and dispersive power $\omega_1=0.02$ is to be combined with a second lens of dispersive power $\omega_2=0.03$ to form an achromatic combination. The focal length of the second lens must be
questions.explanation: Achromatism requires $\dfrac{\omega_1}{f_1}+\dfrac{\omega_2}{f_2}=0 \Rightarrow f_2=-\dfrac{\omega_2f_1}{\omega_1}=-\dfrac{0.03\times10}{0.02}=-15$ cm (a diverging lens).
questions.trick: Achromatism condition: $\omega_1/f_1+\omega_2/f_2=0$ — solve for the unknown $f$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Two thin convex and concave lenses are placed in contact to form an achromatic combination. If both lenses are made of the same material (same dispersive power), then
options: the combination is impossible only if the focal lengths differ
the two focal lengths must be equal and of the same sign, doubling the power
the two focal lengths must be equal in magnitude but opposite in sign, so the net power is zero
achromatism needs unequal dispersive powers, so any pair of focal lengths works here
questions.explanation: Achromatism requires $\dfrac{\omega_1}{f_1}+\dfrac{\omega_2}{f_2}=0$. If $\omega_1=\omega_2$ (same material), this forces $f_1=-f_2$, so the net power $1/f_1+1/f_2=0$ — the combination has no focusing ability, making it useless despite being achromatic.
questions.trick: Achromatic pair needs different materials; same material forces $f_1=-f_2$, net power zero.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Total internal reflection occurs when light travels
options: from denser to rarer medium with angle of incidence less than the critical angle
from rarer to denser medium with angle of incidence greater than the critical angle
from rarer to denser medium at any angle
from denser to rarer medium with angle of incidence greater than the critical angle
questions.explanation: Both conditions are needed: denser → rarer and $i > C$.
questions.trick: TIR needs BOTH conditions: denser to rarer AND angle greater than critical angle.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A biconvex lens has both faces of radius of curvature 10 cm and is made of glass with $n=1.5$. Its focal length is
questions.explanation: $\dfrac1f=(n-1)\left(\dfrac1{R_1}-\dfrac1{R_2}\right)=0.5\left(\dfrac1{10}-\dfrac1{-10}\right)=0.5\times0.2=0.1 \Rightarrow f=10$ cm.
questions.trick: Biconvex, equal radii: $1/f=(n-1)(2/R)$ — $R_1$ positive, $R_2$ negative, don't cancel.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A person suffering from myopia (short-sightedness) can see nearby objects clearly but not distant objects. This defect is corrected using a
questions.explanation: In myopia the image of a distant object forms in front of the retina; a diverging (concave) lens shifts it back onto the retina.
questions.trick: Myopia (far objects blurry) needs a concave lens; hypermetropia needs a convex lens.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A hypermetropic eye has its near point at 50 cm instead of 25 cm. The power of the corrective lens needed so that an object at 25 cm forms a virtual image at 50 cm is
questions.explanation: $\dfrac1v-\dfrac1u=\dfrac1f$: with $u=-25$ cm, $v=-50$ cm, $\dfrac1f=-\dfrac1{50}+\dfrac1{25}=\dfrac1{50}$, so $f=50$ cm $=0.5$ m and $P=+2$ D.
questions.trick: Hypermetropia fix: apply $1/f=1/v-1/u$ with the given near points, then $P=1/f$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A convex spherical surface of radius 20 cm separates air ($n=1$) from glass ($n=1.5$). An object is placed 100 cm from the surface in air. Using $\dfrac{n_2}{v}-\dfrac{n_1}{u}=\dfrac{n_2-n_1}{R}$, the image distance is
questions.trick: Curved surface: $n_2/v-n_1/u=(n_2-n_1)/R$ — plug in signs carefully.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: In a primary rainbow, the colours violet and red appear
options: with violet on the inner edge of the arc and red on the outer edge
with red on the inner edge of the arc and violet on the outer edge
with violet on top and red at the bottom of the arc
at the same position, since both deviate equally
questions.explanation: Violet light emerges from raindrops at a smaller angle from the direction of sunlight than red, so violet appears on the inner edge and red on the outer edge of a primary rainbow.
questions.trick: Primary rainbow: violet deviates most, so it appears on the inner arc.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A convex lens of glass ($n = 1.5$) has focal length 20 cm in air. Its focal length in water ($n = 4/3$) is
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{f_w}{f_a} = \dfrac{n_g - 1}{n_g/n_w - 1} = \dfrac{0.5}{1.125 - 1} = 4 \Rightarrow f_w = 80$ cm.
questions.trick: Lens in water: use $n_{rel}=n_g/n_m$ in the lens-maker equation; $f$ roughly quadruples.
questions.tip: Focal length of a glass lens becomes about 4 times in water.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A ray of light enters perpendicular to one face of a 45°-45°-90° glass prism ($n=1.5$) and strikes the hypotenuse face at 45°, which exceeds the critical angle (about 41.8°), so it undergoes total internal reflection and emerges perpendicular to the other short face. The ray has been turned through
questions.explanation: The single total internal reflection at the hypotenuse bends the ray by 90°, which is why such prisms are used in binoculars and periscopes instead of mirrors.
questions.trick: 45-45-90 TIR prism: light undergoes total internal reflection and turns exactly 90°.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The sky appears blue because
options: air molecules absorb all colours except blue
blue light travels faster than other colours in air
red light is scattered more than blue light
shorter wavelengths (blue) are scattered more strongly by air molecules than longer wavelengths (Rayleigh scattering, $\propto 1/\lambda^4$)
questions.explanation: Rayleigh scattering by air molecules is much stronger for shorter wavelengths, so blue light is scattered across the sky far more than red, giving the sky its blue colour.
questions.trick: Rayleigh scattering goes as $1/\lambda^4$ — blue scatters most, hence blue sky.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: In the Cartesian sign convention used for mirrors and lenses, the object distance $u$ for a real object is always taken as
options: dependent on whether the mirror is concave or convex
negative, since it is measured against the direction of incident light
questions.explanation: With incident light taken as travelling in the positive direction, a real object (always in front of the mirror/lens) has $u$ measured backward from the pole/optical centre, so $u$ is negative.
questions.trick: Real object $u$ is always negative — incident light direction is the positive axis.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The image formed by a convex mirror is always
questions.explanation: Convex mirrors have a wide field of view and always form virtual, erect, diminished images — hence used as rear-view mirrors.
questions.trick: Convex mirror: always virtual, erect, diminished — no exceptions, ever.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The refractive index of a medium is $\sqrt2$. Its critical angle is
questions.explanation: $\sin C = 1/n = 1/\sqrt2 \Rightarrow C = 45^\circ$.
questions.trick: $\sin C=1/n$ — plug in $n$, solve the inverse sine directly.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A thin glass plate of thickness 0.01 mm and refractive index 1.5 is introduced in the path of one of the two beams in a YDSE arrangement using light of wavelength 5000 Å. The fringe pattern shifts by
questions.explanation: Number of fringes shifted $n = \dfrac{(\mu-1)t}{\lambda} = \dfrac{0.5\times10^{-5}}{5\times10^{-7}} = 10$.
questions.trick: Fringe shift from a thin plate: $n=(\mu-1)t/\lambda$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Malus's law $I = I_0\cos^2\theta$ applies to light that is
options: unpolarised, incident on a single polariser
already plane polarised, incident on an analyser
questions.explanation: Malus's law gives the intensity transmitted by an analyser when plane-polarised light of intensity $I_0$ (already polarised by a first polariser) falls on it at angle $\theta$ to its axis.
questions.trick: Malus's law needs already-polarised light hitting the analyser, not raw unpolarised light.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: For a clearly visible interference pattern on a screen, the two coherent sources should ideally be
options: close together, with the screen placed far away
placed at the same location as the screen
as far apart from each other as possible
questions.explanation: Small $d$ and large $D$ give a large, easily observable fringe width $\beta = \lambda D/d$; also, closely spaced sources are easier to keep coherent.
questions.trick: Good fringes need small $d$ (close sources) and large $D$ (far screen).
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Which pair of sources can produce a sustained (observable) interference pattern?
options: Two virtual sources obtained by division of wavefront from a single monochromatic source
Two identical but independently operating laser pointers
questions.explanation: Only sources derived from the same original wavefront (as in YDSE, by division of wavefront) maintain a constant phase relationship and are coherent; independent sources are never coherent.
questions.trick: Only division-of-wavefront sources (same origin) stay coherent — independent ones never do.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: In a single slit diffraction pattern, the width of the central maximum compared to a secondary maximum is
questions.explanation: The central maximum extends between the first minima on either side and is twice as wide as any secondary maximum.
questions.trick: Central maximum is always exactly twice as wide as any secondary maximum.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: In YDSE, if one of the two slits is covered, what is observed on the screen?
options: A single-slit diffraction pattern, not interference fringes
The same interference pattern with half the intensity
questions.explanation: With only one slit open there is no second coherent source to interfere with, so a single-slit diffraction pattern (broad central maximum with weak secondary maxima) is seen instead of equally spaced interference fringes.
questions.trick: Cover one slit and you lose interference, getting plain single-slit diffraction instead.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The optical path length of a slab of thickness 3 mm and refractive index 1.5 is
questions.explanation: Optical path length $= \mu t = 1.5\times3 = 4.5$ mm.
questions.trick: Optical path length $=\mu\times$ geometric thickness — a simple multiply.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A single slit of width 0.3 mm is illuminated by light of wavelength 600 nm. The angular position of the first minimum is approximately
questions.explanation: First minimum: $\sin\theta \approx \theta = \lambda/a = (600\times10^{-9})/(0.3\times10^{-3}) = 2\times10^{-3}$ rad.
questions.trick: Single slit first minimum: $\theta\approx\lambda/a$ (small angle, radians).
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: In a single-slit diffraction experiment, if the slit width is reduced to half its original value (wavelength and screen distance unchanged), the width of the central maximum
questions.explanation: Width of central maximum $\propto 1/a$; halving the slit width $a$ doubles the width of the central maximum.
questions.trick: Central maximum width $\propto1/a$ — halve the slit width, double the width.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: In a YDSE setup, $d = 0.5$ mm, $D = 1.5$ m and $\lambda = 600$ nm. The distance of the 5th bright fringe from the centre is
questions.explanation: $y_n = \dfrac{n\lambda D}{d} = \dfrac{5\times600\times10^{-9}\times1.5}{0.5\times10^{-3}} = 9\times10^{-3}\ \text{m} = 9$ mm.
questions.trick: Bright fringe position: $y_n=n\lambda D/d$ — plug in the fringe number $n$ directly.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The entire YDSE setup is immersed in water of refractive index 4/3. The fringe width
questions.explanation: Wavelength decreases in a denser medium: $\lambda' = \lambda/\mu$, so $\beta' = \beta/\mu$, a decrease by 4/3.
questions.trick: Immersed in a medium: $\beta'=\beta/\mu$ — wavelength shrinks by $\mu$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A 100 W sodium lamp radiates light of wavelength 590 nm uniformly in all directions. The number of photons emitted per second is approximately (take $hc \approx 1.99\times10^{-25}$ J m)
questions.explanation: Energy per photon $= hc/\lambda = 1.99\times10^{-25}/5.9\times10^{-7} \approx 3.37\times10^{-19}$ J. Number of photons per second $= 100/3.37\times10^{-19} \approx 3\times10^{20}$.
questions.trick: Photons per second equal power divided by energy per photon ($hc/\lambda$).
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Photoelectric emission from a metal surface occurs with a time lag of
questions.explanation: Photoelectric emission is essentially instantaneous ($<10^{-9}$ s), consistent with a single photon transferring its energy to a single electron in one interaction.
questions.trick: Photoelectric emission has no time lag — one photon, one electron, instantly.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: In a photoelectric experiment, if the intensity of incident light is increased keeping the frequency constant (above threshold), then
options: maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons increases
questions.explanation: More intensity means more photons per second, ejecting more electrons per second, increasing saturation current; $KE_{max}$ and stopping potential depend only on frequency, not intensity.
questions.trick: Intensity up means only saturation current up; $KE_{max}$ never changes with intensity.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The stopping potential for photoelectrons from a metal is 2 V when light of frequency $\nu$ is used. The maximum speed of the emitted electrons is closest to (take $e/m = 1.76\times10^{11}$ C/kg)
questions.explanation: $\tfrac12 mv^2 = eV_0 \Rightarrow v = \sqrt{2V_0(e/m)} = \sqrt{2\times2\times1.76\times10^{11}} = \sqrt{7.04\times10^{11}} \approx 8.4\times10^{5}$ m/s.
questions.trick: Stopping potential to speed: $v=\sqrt{2V_0(e/m)}$, plug in numbers directly.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The work function of a metal is 2 eV. The threshold frequency for photoelectric emission is (take $h = 6.6\times10^{-34}$ J s, 1 eV $= 1.6\times10^{-19}$ J)
questions.trick: $\nu_0=\phi_0/h$ — divide the work function (in joules) by Planck's constant.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Which observation from the photoelectric effect could NOT be explained by the classical wave theory of light?
options: Light can eject electrons from a metal
Existence of a threshold frequency below which no emission occurs, regardless of intensity
questions.explanation: Classical wave theory predicts that sufficiently intense light of any frequency should eventually eject electrons by accumulating energy, but experiments showed no emission below a threshold frequency no matter how intense — explained only by Einstein's photon (quantum) picture.
questions.trick: A threshold frequency independent of intensity is the wave theory's fatal flaw.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: An electron and a proton are accelerated through the same potential difference. The de Broglie wavelength of the electron compared to the proton is
options: smaller, since electron mass is smaller
equal, since charge is the same magnitude
larger, since electron mass is smaller
questions.explanation: $\lambda = h/\sqrt{2meV}$; since $m_{electron} \ll m_{proton}$, $\lambda_{electron} > \lambda_{proton}$ for the same $V$.
questions.trick: Same $V$: lighter mass (electron) gives a longer de Broglie wavelength.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: In a photoelectric experiment, if the frequency of the incident light is increased while its intensity is kept fixed (above threshold), the I-V graph shows
options: the same stopping potential as before
the same saturation current, but a larger (more negative) stopping potential
questions.explanation: At the same intensity, the same number of photons arrive per second, so saturation current stays the same; but higher frequency gives photoelectrons more kinetic energy, requiring a larger stopping potential to halt them.
questions.trick: Fixed intensity, higher frequency: current unchanged, but $V_0$ rises (more KE).
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A photon and an electron have the same de Broglie wavelength. Then they must have the same
questions.explanation: $\lambda = h/p$ for both; equal $\lambda$ implies equal momentum $p$. Their energies differ since photon energy is $pc$ while electron KE is $p^2/2m$.
questions.trick: Same de Broglie $\lambda$ means same momentum $p=h/\lambda$, not same energy.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The photoelectric effect experiment established which of the following about light?
options: Light travels faster in denser media than in vacuum
Light is purely a wave with no particle-like behaviour
Light behaves as a stream of quanta (photons), each of energy $h\nu$
questions.explanation: The threshold-frequency behaviour and instantaneous emission observed in the photoelectric effect could only be explained by treating light as quanta (photons) of energy $h\nu$, as proposed by Einstein.
questions.trick: The photoelectric effect's whole point: light behaves as quanta of energy $h\nu$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the photoelectric effect is correct?
options: Maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons increases with the intensity of incident light
The threshold frequency of a metal depends on the intensity of the incident light
Photoelectric current depends only on the frequency of incident light
Maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons is independent of intensity but depends on frequency
questions.explanation: By Einstein's equation $KE_{max} = h\nu - \phi_0$, the maximum kinetic energy depends only on frequency and the metal's work function, never on intensity.
questions.trick: $KE_{max}$ depends ONLY on frequency and metal — intensity never enters this formula.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The shortest wavelength (series limit) of the Balmer series of hydrogen is approximately (use $R = 1.097\times10^7\ \text{m}^{-1}$)
questions.explanation: Series limit corresponds to $n_2\to\infty$: $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{4}-0\right) = R/4 \approx 2.74\times10^6\ \text{m}^{-1}$, so $\lambda \approx 365$ nm.
questions.trick: Balmer series limit: $1/\lambda=R/4$ — set $n_2\to\infty$, $n_1=2$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The wavelength of the first line of the Balmer series (transition $n=3 \to n=2$) in hydrogen is close to (use $R = 1.097\times10^7\ \text{m}^{-1}$)
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\dfrac{1}{4}-\dfrac{1}{9}\right) = R\times\dfrac{5}{36} = 1.097\times10^7\times0.1389 \approx 1.524\times10^6\ \text{m}^{-1}$, so $\lambda \approx 656$ nm (H-alpha line).
questions.trick: Balmer 656 nm (H-alpha) is the classic $3\to2$ transition, worth memorising directly.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The angular momentum of the electron in the third Bohr orbit ($n=3$) of hydrogen is
questions.explanation: By Bohr's quantisation rule, $L = nh/2\pi$; for $n=3$, $L = 3h/2\pi$.
questions.trick: Angular momentum for $n=3$: just plug into $L=nh/2\pi$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: An electron in a hydrogen atom has total energy $-0.85$ eV. The value of the principal quantum number $n$ for this state is
questions.trick: Given $E_n$, solve $n^2=13.6/|E_n|$ to find the quantum number.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The frequency of revolution of the electron in the $n$th Bohr orbit of hydrogen varies as
questions.explanation: Since $v_n \propto 1/n$ and $r_n \propto n^2$, the revolution frequency $f = v_n/(2\pi r_n) \propto 1/n^3$.
questions.trick: Revolution frequency $f=v/(2\pi r)\propto1/n^3$ — combine the $v_n$ and $r_n$ laws.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The de Broglie wavelength of the electron in the $n$th Bohr orbit is related to the orbit's circumference by
questions.explanation: Bohr's quantisation $mvr = nh/2\pi$ combined with de Broglie's $\lambda = h/mv$ gives $2\pi r_n = n\lambda$ — an integer number of de Broglie wavelengths fit the orbit, providing a physical basis for quantisation.
questions.trick: Bohr plus de Broglie: $2\pi r_n=n\lambda$ — integer wavelengths fit the orbit exactly.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A hydrogen atom is excited from its ground state to $n=3$. The number of possible wavelengths that can be emitted as it returns to the ground state is
questions.explanation: $\dfrac{n(n-1)}{2} = \dfrac{3\times2}{2} = 3$ possible transitions/wavelengths: $3\to2$, $2\to1$, $3\to1$.
questions.trick: 3 possible transitions from $n=3$ to ground: $3(3-1)/2=3$ — just compute directly.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The energy of the photon emitted during the transition $n=2 \to n=1$ in a singly ionised helium atom (Z=2) is
questions.trick: For ions, compute $E_n=-13.6Z^2/n^2$ first, then subtract for $\Delta E$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A hydrogen spectral line has wavelength 486 nm, one of the well-known Balmer lines. This corresponds to the transition
questions.explanation: The Balmer line at 486 nm (H-beta) arises from the transition $n=4 \to n=2$.
questions.trick: 486 nm (H-beta) is the specific $4\to2$ Balmer transition — a memorisable pair.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Bohr's postulate that electrons revolve in certain stable orbits without radiating energy directly contradicts
options: the law of conservation of charge
classical electromagnetic theory, which predicts that an accelerating charge should continuously radiate energy
questions.explanation: Classically, an electron moving in a circular orbit is accelerating and should radiate energy continuously, spiralling into the nucleus; Bohr's postulate of non-radiating stationary orbits was an ad hoc departure from classical theory needed to explain atomic stability.
questions.trick: Bohr's 'no radiation' postulate directly defies classical EM theory — that's the point.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The distance of closest approach of an alpha particle to a nucleus is inversely proportional to its kinetic energy $E_k$. If $E_k$ is doubled, the distance of closest approach
questions.explanation: $r_0 = \dfrac{2kZe^2}{E_k} \propto 1/E_k$, so doubling the kinetic energy halves the distance of closest approach.
questions.trick: Doubling KE halves the closest-approach distance ($r_0\propto1/E_k$).
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Isobars are nuclei that have
options: the same neutron number, different atomic numbers
the same mass number, different atomic numbers
the same number of protons and neutrons
the same atomic number, different mass numbers
questions.explanation: Isobars share the same mass number $A$ but differ in atomic number $Z$ (and hence in the number of protons and neutrons); this is distinct from isotopes, which share the same $Z$.
questions.trick: Isobars share mass number $A$, NOT atomic number — opposite of isotopes.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A radioactive sample decays such that $N/N_0 = 1/e^2$ after time $t$. The value of $\lambda t$ is
questions.explanation: $N/N_0 = e^{-\lambda t} = e^{-2} \Rightarrow \lambda t = 2$.
questions.trick: Directly equate exponents: $N/N_0=e^{-\lambda t}$, so $\lambda t=2$ matches $e^{-2}$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Which of the following correctly ranks the penetrating power of alpha, beta and gamma radiation from LEAST to MOST penetrating?
questions.explanation: Alpha particles are stopped by paper/skin, beta particles need a few mm of aluminium, while gamma rays require thick lead or concrete; so penetrating power increases as alpha < beta < gamma.
questions.trick: Penetrating power: alpha (paper) less than beta (Al foil) less than gamma (thick lead).
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The mass defect of a nucleus refers to
options: the mass of the electron cloud
the loss of mass number during fission
the difference between the mass of the nucleus and the sum of masses of its free constituent nucleons
the mass lost due to radioactive decay
questions.explanation: Mass defect $\Delta m = Zm_p + Nm_n - M_{nucleus}$; this 'missing' mass appears as the binding energy holding the nucleus together.
questions.trick: Mass defect is (sum of free nucleon masses) minus actual nucleus mass — always positive.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: 1 atomic mass unit (u) is equivalent to an energy of
questions.explanation: By $E = \Delta m c^2$, 1 u $= 1.66\times10^{-27}$ kg corresponds to 931.5 MeV.
questions.trick: 1 u equals 931.5 MeV — the single most memorised nuclear conversion factor.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The mean life $\tau$ of a radioactive substance is related to its half-life $T_{1/2}$ by
questions.trick: $\tau=T_{1/2}/0.693\approx1.44\,T_{1/2}$ — mean life is always a bit longer.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A self-sustained chain reaction in a nuclear reactor is maintained when the neutron multiplication factor $k$ equals
questions.explanation: When $k=1$ (critical), the number of neutrons causing fission in successive generations stays constant, sustaining a steady chain reaction; $k<1$ is subcritical (reaction dies out) and $k>1$ is supercritical (reaction grows uncontrollably).
questions.trick: Chain reaction: $k=1$ steady, $k<1$ dies out, $k>1$ runs away — memorise all three.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A radioactive sample decays for a time equal to twice its mean life ($t=2\tau$). The fraction of the original sample remaining is approximately
questions.explanation: $N/N_0 = e^{-t/\tau} = e^{-2} \approx 0.135$, i.e. about 13.5% remains.
questions.trick: $t=2\tau$ gives $N/N_0=e^{-2}\approx13.5\%$ — memorise this exponential value.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The SI unit of the radioactive decay constant $\lambda$ is
questions.explanation: From $N=N_0e^{-\lambda t}$, the exponent must be dimensionless, so $\lambda$ has units of inverse time, i.e. $s^{-1}$.
questions.trick: The decay exponent must be dimensionless, so $\lambda$ always has units of $s^{-1}$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A nucleus of mass number 240 (binding energy per nucleon 7.6 MeV) splits into two fragments with a combined mass number of 240 and an average binding energy per nucleon of about 8.5 MeV. The approximate energy released per fission event is
questions.explanation: Total binding energy before $\approx 240\times7.6 = 1824$ MeV; after $\approx 240\times8.5 = 2040$ MeV. Energy released $\approx 2040-1824 = 216$ MeV.
questions.trick: Fission energy equals (total BE after) minus (total BE before), using $BE/A\times A$.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Which of the following correctly ranks the ionising power of alpha, beta and gamma radiation from MOST to LEAST?
questions.explanation: Alpha particles, being heavy and doubly charged, ionise matter most strongly over a short path; gamma rays, being uncharged and highly penetrating, ionise the least per unit path length. Order: alpha > beta > gamma.
questions.trick: Ionising power is the REVERSE of penetrating power: alpha greater than beta greater than gamma.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: In a common-emitter transistor amplifier with $\beta = 100$, $R_{in} = 1$ k$\Omega$ and $R_C = 4$ k$\Omega$, the voltage gain is
questions.explanation: $A_v = \beta\dfrac{R_C}{R_{in}} = 100\times\dfrac{4}{1} = 400$.
questions.trick: $A_v=\beta\times R_C/R_{in}$ — multiply the gain by the resistor ratio directly.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A photodiode is normally operated in
questions.explanation: A photodiode is reverse-biased so that the small reverse saturation current (otherwise negligible) increases measurably and linearly with the intensity of incident light, useful for light detection.
questions.trick: Photodiode is always reverse-biased; current scales with light intensity.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: A half-wave rectifier circuit
options: uses 2 diodes and rectifies both halves of the input cycle
uses 1 diode and rectifies both halves
uses 4 diodes but rectifies only one half
uses 1 diode and rectifies only one half of the input cycle
questions.explanation: A half-wave rectifier uses a single diode, which conducts during only one half of the AC input cycle, blocking the other half.
questions.trick: Half-wave uses 1 diode, only ONE half-cycle conducts — the other is wasted.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: If the AC input frequency to a full-wave rectifier is $f$, the ripple frequency present in its output is
questions.explanation: A full-wave rectifier produces one output pulse for each half-cycle of the input, so the output repeats twice per input cycle, giving a ripple frequency of $2f$.
questions.trick: Full-wave rectifier ripple frequency is $2f$ — double the input frequency.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: In a transistor, the relation between emitter, base and collector currents is
questions.explanation: By Kirchhoff's current law applied to the transistor, the emitter current splits into base and collector currents: $I_E = I_B + I_C$.
questions.trick: $I_E=I_B+I_C$ — emitter current always splits into base plus collector.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: In the energy band picture, an insulator has a very large energy gap because
options: electrons need a very large amount of energy to jump from the (full) valence band to the (empty) conduction band
the conduction band overlaps the valence band
questions.explanation: In insulators, the gap between the filled valence band and empty conduction band is large (typically >3 eV), so thermal or ordinary electric energy is insufficient to make electrons conduct, unlike in semiconductors or conductors.
questions.trick: An insulator's huge gap simply means electrons can't jump valence to conduction band.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The Boolean expression for the output $Y$ of a two-input OR gate with inputs $A$ and $B$ is
questions.explanation: An OR gate gives HIGH output if either or both inputs are HIGH, represented as $Y = A+B$.
questions.trick: OR gate: $Y=A+B$ — HIGH if EITHER input is HIGH.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: In a p-n junction diode under forward bias, the width of the depletion region
questions.explanation: Forward bias opposes the built-in potential barrier, pushing majority carriers into the junction and narrowing the depletion region, allowing current to flow easily.
questions.trick: Forward bias narrows the depletion region — barrier opposed, carriers pushed in.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: In the common collector (emitter follower) transistor configuration, the voltage gain is
questions.explanation: The common collector configuration has high current gain but a voltage gain of nearly 1 (the output follows the input voltage, hence 'emitter follower'), making it useful for impedance matching rather than voltage amplification.
questions.trick: Common collector (emitter follower): voltage gain always about 1, used for impedance matching.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Doping silicon with a pentavalent impurity like phosphorus produces
options: an n-type semiconductor with electrons as majority carriers
a p-type semiconductor with holes as majority carriers
questions.explanation: Phosphorus has 5 valence electrons; 4 bond with silicon, leaving one extra loosely bound electron, giving an n-type semiconductor with electrons as majority carriers.
questions.trick: Pentavalent dopant gives an extra electron — n-type, majority carrier electrons.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The small reverse saturation current in a p-n junction diode is caused by
options: minority carriers, and it is nearly independent of the reverse voltage (though it increases with temperature)
majority carriers, and it increases sharply with reverse voltage
the drift of majority carriers across the depletion layer
questions.explanation: Under reverse bias, only the small number of thermally generated minority carriers are swept across the junction, giving a current that is almost independent of the applied reverse voltage but rises with temperature (more thermal generation).
questions.trick: Reverse saturation current: minority carriers, nearly voltage-independent, rises with temperature.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The typical order of magnitude of current in a forward-biased silicon diode, compared to that in the same diode reverse-biased, is
options: mA in forward bias; µA in reverse bias
A in forward bias; mA in reverse bias
µA in forward bias; nA in reverse bias
µA in forward bias; mA in reverse bias
questions.explanation: A forward-biased diode conducts appreciable current, typically in the milliampere range, while a reverse-biased diode carries only a tiny leakage current, typically in the microampere range.
questions.trick: Forward diode current is in mA; reverse is in µA — three orders of magnitude apart.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The common base (CB) transistor configuration is characterised by
options: an output that is 180° out of phase with the input
being used mainly because it gives a very high current gain
low input impedance and high output impedance, with current gain ($\alpha$) less than 1
questions.explanation: In common base configuration, the input (emitter-base) impedance is low and the output (base-collector) impedance is high, and the current gain $\alpha = I_C/I_E$ is always slightly less than 1; the output voltage is in phase with the input.
questions.trick: Common base: low input impedance, high output impedance, $\alpha<1$ always.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Which of the following is a universal logic gate (can implement any other gate)?
questions.explanation: NAND (and NOR) gates are universal — any logic function, including AND, OR, and NOT, can be built using only NAND gates.
questions.trick: NAND and NOR are the two universal gates — memorise both, not just one.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: Doping silicon with a trivalent impurity such as boron produces
options: a p-type semiconductor with holes as majority carriers
an n-type semiconductor with electrons as majority carriers
questions.explanation: Boron has only 3 valence electrons; it can form only 3 covalent bonds with silicon, leaving a hole in the fourth bond, giving a p-type semiconductor with holes as majority carriers.
questions.trick: Trivalent dopant creates a missing electron (hole) — p-type, majority carrier holes.
questions.subject: physics

questions.q: The main difference between avalanche breakdown and Zener breakdown in a diode is that
options: Zener breakdown requires no electric field at all
avalanche breakdown occurs only in forward bias

avalanche breakdown occurs by carrier multiplication via collisions in a lightly doped junction with a wide depletion region, while Zener breakdown occurs by direct field-induced rupture of covalent bonds in a heavily doped, narrow-depletion junction
the two terms are always exactly synonymous
questions.explanation: Avalanche breakdown relies on accelerated carriers colliding with lattice atoms to multiply charge carriers (occurs in lightly doped, wider depletion diodes); Zener breakdown occurs when a very strong electric field in a heavily doped, narrow junction directly breaks covalent bonds, releasing carriers.
questions.trick: Avalanche means carrier multiplication (lightly doped); Zener means direct bond-breaking (heavily doped).
questions.subject: physics
